items.title: Implement ISO/IEC 27001 in a fictional IT company
items.background: Meridian IT Services Pvt. Ltd. is a fictional 1,400-person information technology services company headquartered in Bengaluru, with delivery centres in Pune and Hyderabad and client operations running 24x7 from two offshore follow-the-sun pods. It maintains systems for a dozen banks and two healthcare clients, most of which are hosted on client-managed infrastructure, but its own service management, ticketing, source control and CI/CD platforms run across a mix of on-premises virtual machines, a public cloud tenant and two co-located racks in a Chennai data centre. The company is ISO 9001 certified and has a well-run HR function, but its management system documentation is inconsistent: each delivery centre maintains its own local variant of the access-control and incident procedures, there is no single ISMS scope, no Statement of Applicability, and no documented risk assessment method. Twenty-two months ago an incident led to a client-side data exposure that was reported under a client contract's 48-hour notification clause; the client retained an external firm, no root cause was ever recorded, and remediation was closed out in a spreadsheet. A large European healthcare client has now made ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification of Meridian's managed service operations a contractual precondition for a four-year managed services renewal worth roughly 40 percent of group revenue, and the contract is expected to be signed within nine months. Internal audit tested access provisioning for two delivery centres and found eleven leaver accounts still active at termination across four systems. The board has approved a budget of 42 lakh rupees over two years, appointed a new Head of Information Security with a COO reporting line, and mandated certification of the managed services and shared services scope rather than the whole company. Because the previous Head resigned in protest at how remediation was being tracked, the board is also watching whether this programme produces evidence rather than documents.
items.scope: In scope: the managed services delivery centres in Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad, the shared services function including IT operations and application support, the Chennai data centre hosting Meridian-owned infrastructure, the cloud tenant used for the ticketing, source control and CI/CD platforms, and all personnel supporting those functions. Also in scope is the management system machinery required by ISO/IEC 27001 clauses 4 to 10, namely scope, risk assessment, Statement of Applicability, competence, documented information, internal audit, management review and improvement. Out of scope: client-owned infrastructure and client applications on which services are delivered; the corporate functions of human resources, finance, legal and administration, except where they provide services to in-scope functions; Meridian's offices outside the three delivery centres; and the enterprise risk register and fraud controls, which sit under a separate ERM programme. The company's own commercial software product entity is out of scope as a separate legal entity, and its exclusion must be justified against clause 4.3.
objectives: Define and document the ISMS scope, boundaries and exclusions, and defend each exclusion against the requirements of clause 4.3 and the client contract.
Select, document and actually operate a risk assessment method that produces a risk register with a risk treatment plan, named owners and due dates.
Establish the complete Annex A control set and produce a Statement of Applicability that justifies every control marked not applicable.
Stand up the operating management system, including a risk-based internal audit programme and a first management review cycle run on real evidence.
Design an evidence strategy so that each applicable control has a repeatable, artefact-based proof rather than an annual attestation.
Rebuild incident management to meet the contractual 48-hour notification clock, including a decision tree for when a notification is triggered.
Produce a credible implementation roadmap with sequencing, dependencies, resourcing and a costed budget that fits the approved envelope.
Prepare the organisation for a Stage 1 and Stage 2 certification audit by an accredited certification body.
startingInformation: Meridian has 1,400 employees: 980 in delivery, 140 in shared services and 280 in corporate functions. Three sites plus a Chennai data centre are candidates for certification.
No documented ISMS scope exists. Three sites each claim to follow the ISMS but refer to different versions of the same policy.

The information security function has nine people: a Head of Information Security (three months in post), two security engineers, one IAM specialist, one cloud engineer, one vulnerability analyst, one SOC lead, one security awareness manager and one empty GRC analyst role, which is the role you are filling.
Internal audit tested access provisioning at two delivery centres and found eleven leaver accounts still active at termination across four systems.
No risk assessment method exists. The last attempt was a spreadsheet of 'known threats' with no likelihood or impact scale, no risk criteria and no treatment options.
The Chennai data centre hosts 41 internally delivered applications, nine of them on hardware the vendor confirmed is out of vendor support since 2024.
The cloud tenant has four AWS accounts with no organisation-level landing zone, and 180 IAM identities with no evidence of any quarterly access review.

Clause 9.3 of the healthcare client's managed services agreement requires ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification within 12 months of signature, annual surveillance thereafter, 48-hour incident notification and quarterly evidence of control operation.
Approved budget is 42 lakh rupees over 24 months, with a possible additional 18 lakh if the board accepts a phased certification scope.
The only certification body quote received so far is 11.5 lakh rupees for Stage 1, Stage 2 and year-one surveillance, with recertification surveillance in year two.
The 22-month-old client data exposure has a legal file but no incident record and no root cause analysis; the previous Head closed it as 'remediated' with no artefact.
The Head of Information Security reports to the COO, not to the board; the CRO owns enterprise risk and has asked for a single federated view of security risk.
activities: Extract every auditable and notifiable obligation from clause 9.3 of the healthcare client agreement and turn it into a requirements register mapped to ISMS clauses.
Define the ISMS scope statement, organisational and virtual boundaries, excluded sites and excluded entities, and document the justification for each exclusion.
Build the interested parties register and complete a legal and regulatory requirements analysis covering the Indian context as well as the client contract.
Select and document the risk assessment methodology: scales, risk criteria, evaluation method, treatment options and acceptance authority.
Run risk assessment workshops with the three delivery centre heads, the cloud engineer, the SOC lead and the shared services lead, and produce the risk register.
Produce the risk treatment plan with named owners, due dates, acceptance authority and a cost reconciliation against the 42 lakh envelope.
Design the risk-based internal audit programme and run the first audit cycle, including a re-test of the leaver-access finding.
Produce the Statement of Applicability covering all 93 Annex A controls, with a genuine justification for every control marked not applicable.
Design the control evidence catalogue and implement collection mechanics for the top 25 controls, including the quarterly access review and the 48-hour notification log.
Rebuild the incident management procedure with severity criteria, a 48-hour notification decision tree and customer communication templates.
Plan and run a management review using real evidence from the audit, the risk register, the incident log and the treatment plan.
Build the implementation roadmap with dependencies, resourcing, cost, certification body engagement and Stage 1 readiness gating.
Run a mock Stage 1 audit internally and close or re-plan the gaps it surfaces.
deliverables: ISMS scope statement with documented boundaries, excluded sites and justified exclusions
Requirements register mapping client contractual obligations to ISO/IEC 27001 clauses
Documented ISMS risk assessment methodology and the completed ISMS risk register
Risk treatment plan with named owners, due dates, acceptance authority and cost reconciliation to the approved budget
Signed Statement of Applicability covering all 93 Annex A controls with per-control justification
Internal audit programme plus the completed first-cycle internal audit report, findings and agreed management actions
Control evidence catalogue and implementation plan for the top 25 controls with named owners
Incident management procedure including the 48-hour client notification decision tree and log template
Eighteen-month implementation roadmap with resourcing, cost, dependencies and certification body engagement plan
evaluationCriteria: Scope definition is defensible: boundaries are explicit, exclusions are justified against clause 4.3 and the contractual requirement, and a reader can tell in one sentence what is and is not certified.

The risk assessment uses a documented, repeatable method. Scales, risk criteria and treatment options are explicit, and the register shows traceability from threat to control to residual risk and owner.
The Statement of Applicability addresses all 93 controls with genuine justification rather than blanket exclusions, and controls marked not applicable are supported by a stated reason.
The treatment plan is operationally credible: owners are real roles rather than the learner, sequencing respects dependencies, and the cost fits the stated budget with trade-offs stated openly.
Evidence is specified in operational terms: what artefact proves each control, who produces it, how frequently, where it is retained and for how long.

Risk reasoning is specific to Meridian's actual estate, citing the legacy Chennai hardware, the four ungoverned cloud accounts, the follow-the-sun pod handover and the leaver-access history, rather than generic threats.
The audit and management review are operating cycles rather than one-off exercises, with sampling approach, independence rule, escalation path and follow-up tracking defined.
The incident procedure meets the 48-hour contractual clock and states clearly what triggers a notification, who decides, and what happens when the clock and the facts conflict.
The roadmap distinguishes what will be certified in scope at Stage 2 from what will follow, and explains the phased scope decision to the board in risk language.
The submission separates a short board-facing summary from the technical annexes, and states plainly what will not be done in the first year and why.
items.modelSolution:
The approach that survives contact with a certification body is to treat certification as the by-product of running a management system rather than the goal itself. Meridian has already failed once by producing documents, so the first deliverable is not a policy set; it is a decision about what is actually in scope and what evidence will demonstrate the controls.

Start with the contract, not the standard. Clause 9.3 is the client's real requirement, and it is narrower and sharper than ISO 27001. Read it with the account manager and build a requirements register: certification within 12 months of signature, annual surveillance, 48-hour incident notification, and quarterly evidence of control operation. That last clause is the most commercially dangerous item because it obliges Meridian to prove operation, not design, every quarter. From that register, the ISMS scope follows. The managed services and shared services functions in three cities plus the Chennai data centre and the cloud tenant go in. The client-owned infrastructure goes out because Meridian cannot operate controls over assets it does not own, and that exclusion must be justified in the scope statement, not just implied. HR, finance and legal go out with the caveat that where they provide services to in-scope functions, the relevant controls are pulled back in. The commercial software entity is out as a separate legal entity, and again the exclusion is written down. The scope statement should be one page, approved by the COO, and reused verbatim in the certification body contract, because a mismatch between what the CB audits and what the contract requires is the single most common cause of a failed Stage 2.

Then build the risk method before any risk content. Meridian's failure was not that threats were unknown, it was that there was no scale, no criteria and no decision rights. A workable method for a 1,400-person services firm is a five-by-five likelihood and impact grid with financial and regulatory impact weighted above reputational impact, an explicit low/medium/high band, four treatment options including accept, and named acceptance authority at COO level for medium and above. Document it once, apply it in workshops rather than by questionnaire, and record the workshop attendance and the challenge that took place, because internal audit will test whether the assessment was a conversation or a form-filling exercise. Run the workshops with the three delivery centre heads, not with a proxy. The follow-the-sun pod handover between Hyderabad and Pune is exactly the kind of risk that a questionnaire never surfaces and a five-minute question in a workshop does.

The risk register will be short and specific if done properly. Legacy hardware in Chennai with nine applications out of vendor support is a register entry, not a threat catalogue entry. Four cloud accounts with no landing zone and 180 identities with no access review is a register entry, and it also drives the IAM build. The eleven leaver accounts still active is the most embarrassing artefact in the file and it should be treated as a current risk with a treatment already partly implemented, not as a closed finding.

Turn the register into a treatment plan and let the budget be honest. At 42 lakh over 24 months, Meridian cannot do everything. The correct trade-off is to fund the controls that the contract explicitly requires quarterly evidence for, plus the identity and access work that removes the largest single exposure, and to explicitly defer the legacy Chennai hardware refresh with a compensating control and a dated risk acceptance from the COO. A plan that claims to do everything and then quietly slips will be read by the board as exactly the pattern that lost them their previous Head.

The Statement of Applicability is where most first-time implementations fail, because it is treated as a spreadsheet exercise. It is not; it is the document that proves you know your own estate. Every one of the 93 Annex A controls gets a status, a justification and, where not applicable, a stated reason tied to Meridian's situation. Exclusion of A.8.16 monitoring activities, for example, requires an explanation of what monitoring does exist and why it is adequate, not the single word 'not applicable'. Controls that are excluded still need their risk addressed by another route, so the SoA and the risk register have to be cross-referenced.

Design the evidence catalogue alongside the SoA, not afterwards. For the top 25 controls, name the artefact, the system it comes from, the production frequency, the owner, the retention period and the storage location. Quarterly access review, joiner-mover-leaver reports, vulnerability scan results, incident notification log, backup restore test records, supplier assurance evidence. Build the mechanics so evidence is captured as a by-product of operating the control rather than assembled a week before an audit. Evidence designed in advance is the single biggest determinant of whether Stage 1 goes smoothly.

Rebuild incident management as a control, not a document. Severity definitions tied to the contractual clock, a decision tree that makes the notification call within hours rather than days, named roles for the decision, customer communication templates and a log. The past incident failed here, and the client will test this specific control during surveillance. Run it as a live tabletop once, because a decision tree that has never been walked is a hypothesis.

Internal audit has to be genuinely risk-based, which means the programme is chosen from the risk register, executed by people independent of the activity, and followed up to closure. Use the leaver-access finding as the first re-test, because the board already knows about it and the result will set the tone.

Finally, the management review. Convene it with real inputs: risk register movement, audit findings, incident log, treatment plan status, supplier assurance status, and interested party feedback including the client's audit findings. Minutes that record real decisions and show that decisions changed something are what distinguish a management system from a management theatre. Produce a two-page board summary that says what is on track, what is late, what was accepted and who accepted it. That summary, not the SoA, is what the board will read.

On cost, Stage 1 and Stage 2 with the quoted body is 11.5 lakh, leaving roughly 30 lakh for people, tools and remediation. That is enough for the IAM work, the evidence tooling and the callback controls, and it is not enough for the Chennai hardware refresh. Say that plainly, and let the COO accept the legacy risk in writing for twelve months.
items.managementFeedback:
This is a materially better piece of work than the last attempt, and I can tell you why: you started from the client contract instead of the standard, which is how real implementations succeed. The scope statement is short, the exclusions are argued rather than asserted, and I can finally answer a client question about what is covered without opening three documents. The requirements register mapping clause 9.3 to specific ISMS clauses is exactly the artefact I would put in front of the account manager.

Where I push back is the legacy Chennai hardware. Your treatment plan defers it with a compensating control and a risk acceptance from me, which is defensible for twelve months, but I have to be honest with you: I do not accept it indefinitely and I will be asked at the next board meeting why nine applications are running on unsupported platforms while we hold a client contract that references certification. You have given me the argument I need, but you need to give me the date by which it is funded or removed, because a risk acceptance without an expiry date is just a way of not making a decision. Fix that in the treatment plan.

The second thing is evidence. You have specified what artefact proves each control and who produces it, which is right, but several of the owners you have named are people who have never been asked whether they can produce that artefact weekly without it becoming a job in itself. Get their agreement before the next review, and where an owner says no, change the control or the frequency, not the document.

On the Statement of Applicability, the justification for excluding monitoring activities reads like it was written by someone who has never watched our SOC. The reasoning needs to name what monitoring we actually run and why it is proportionate. A certification body auditor will ask a follow-up question on exactly that line.

What would make me promote you: you are the first person in eighteen months who has brought me a plan with a number attached to a risk instead of a spreadsheet with a status column. If you keep that discipline when the project gets hard, in month seven when the delivery centre managers start missing the internal audit dates, this is a different programme and I will say so to the board.

items.title: Conduct an enterprise cybersecurity risk assessment
items.background: Vanguard Financial Services Ltd. is a fictional 5,000-employee universal bank based in Mumbai, providing retail and corporate banking through 640 branches, a 180-person IT operations team and a 24x7 security operations centre that moved into a new facility eleven months ago. Its estate spans a Chennai data centre, two co-location sites, a customer-facing internet and mobile banking platform with 3.1 million registered users, a corporate banking platform used by 4,200 corporate clients, a payments hub that clears to the domestic scheme, and an increasing portfolio of cloud workloads on a single hyperscaler across three accounts. It is supervised by the Reserve Bank of India and is subject to the information security and cyber security framework directions issued by the regulator, which require a board-approved information security policy, a Chief Information Security Officer reporting to the board, and a documented risk assessment with independent validation at least once every three years. Six weeks ago the bank received an anonymous complaint alleging that a retired employee retained access to a data warehouse used for customer analytics, and while preliminary work suggests the access was removed within a week of retirement, no system logs were retained long enough to prove when it was used. In the same month the bank was told by its cloud provider that a misconfiguration in one of the three accounts had left customer profile attributes readable by a broad IAM role for eleven days before detection. A new Chief Risk Officer arrived in March and has asked for a single enterprise view of cyber risk that reconciles the security team's technical registers with the enterprise risk register, and she has made the assessment a condition of her own appointment. The Chief Information Security Officer wants an assessment that will survive a regulatory examination rather than a security posture scorecard.
items.scope: In scope: all information assets and supporting facilities of the bank, including the Chennai data centre and both co-location sites, the internet and mobile banking platform, the corporate banking platform, the payments hub, all three cloud accounts, the customer analytics data warehouse, the SOC tooling, the 640-branch estate and its WAN, end-user computing, and the people and third parties who administer these assets. Also in scope is the assessment method itself, the risk treatment options and the reporting that follows. Out of scope: the risk of the bank's own credit, market and liquidity exposures, which are owned by the CRO and covered by the enterprise risk assessment; the commercial strategy and pricing decisions of the business; the physical security of branch premises beyond a light-touch view taken as an input from the physical security team; and the vendor's own products and internal controls, which are addressed through third-party assessment rather than directly. Regulatory reporting obligations arising from findings are noted but the filing itself is out of scope.
objectives: Define the assessment scope, the asset and system inventory it relies on, and the explicit gaps in that inventory.
Select and document an assessment method that produces defensible risk ratings and a repeatable baseline.
Assess the maturity of cyber risk governance, including board reporting, risk appetite and the three lines model, as well as technical control effectiveness.
Identify the specific cyber risks that matter to Vanguard's business objectives and regulatory obligations, including payments, customer data and the cloud transition.
Produce a risk register that reconciles technical findings with the enterprise risk register and existing risk acceptance decisions.
Evaluate the effectiveness of existing controls by testing a defined sample, not by reading policy documents.
Propose a risk treatment plan with options, costs, owners and sequencing, and distinguish treatments that reduce exposure from treatments that merely transfer it.
Deliver an executive-facing assessment report and a board-level presentation that state the residual risk position plainly.
startingInformation: Vanguard has 5,000 employees, 640 branches, a 180-person IT operations team and a 24x7 SOC of 34 staff including 12 shift analysts.
The CISO reports to the board risk committee quarterly and to the CEO day to day; the CRO owns the enterprise risk register and the risk appetite statement.
The bank operates a Chennai data centre, two co-location sites and three cloud accounts on one hyperscaler; a fourth account has been requested for the payments platform isolation project.

Six weeks ago an anonymous complaint alleged a retired employee retained data warehouse access; access was removed within a week of retirement but 90-day log retention means there is no evidence of use in the interim.
A cloud misconfiguration left customer profile attributes readable by a broad IAM role for eleven days before detection by an external scanner rather than an internal control.
The bank's internal audit function, of 38 staff, audited the branch WAN and the payments hub in the last cycle and raised 41 findings, of which 29 remain open with an average age of 14 months.
An enterprise risk register exists with 118 risks; 6 are classified as above appetite and are owned by business heads, not by IT.

The regulator's framework directions require a board-approved information security policy, CISO board reporting, an annual risk assessment and independent validation at least every three years; the last independent validation was two years ago.
Two registered third parties support core banking and the payment aggregator with the annual certification evidence on file but no contractual right to audit in either case.
Budget available for treatment in this financial year is 9 crore rupees, with a further request possible at mid-year; IT operations headcount is capped.
The CRO has stated that a single reconciled enterprise cyber risk view, reporting monthly rather than quarterly, is the outcome she will be judged on.
activities: Review the regulator's cyber security framework directions and the bank's own policies to extract the mandatory requirements and turn them into an assessment criteria set.
Reconcile the asset inventory from the CMDB, the network diagrams and the cloud configuration exports; document where the three disagree.
Interview the CISO, the IT operations head, the SOC lead, the cloud platform owner, the data protection officer and the two business unit technology heads.
Assess the cyber risk governance maturity, including the three lines model, risk appetite translation, second line independence and committee reporting.

Test a sample of security controls using technique, including privileged access recertification, cloud IAM privilege analysis, logging coverage on the payments hub, branch WAN segmentation and vulnerability management.
Model the attack path for two realistic threat scenarios, an internet-facing credential compromise and a malicious or compromised privileged insider, using the actual asset graph.
Review and score the third-party and insider risk exposure, including access recertification, offboarding data retention and privileged access management across the estate.
Reconcile findings into the enterprise risk register with explicit mapping to existing risks, confirming which risks are already accepted and at what level.
Develop treatment options for each significant finding with cost, effort, dependencies, residual risk and an indicative timeline, and separate true risk reduction from risk transfer.
Run the assessment report through the CRO, the CISO and the CEO's chief of staff, and resolve disagreements in risk rating in writing.
Present the findings and the residual risk position to the board risk committee and capture the decisions, accepted risks and required actions.
deliverables: Assessment scope statement, criteria set and method document with rating scales and confidence levels
Reconciled information asset and system inventory with documented gaps and confidence ratings
Cyber risk governance maturity assessment covering board oversight, three lines model and risk appetite translation
Technical control effectiveness test results for the defined sample, with testing method and evidence references
Two attack path analyses for realistic threat scenarios with the control break points identified
Reconciled enterprise cyber risk register with mapping to existing risks and existing acceptances
Risk treatment plan with options, cost, owner, dependency and residual risk for each significant finding
Assessment report and a board risk committee presentation stating residual risk position and decisions required
evaluationCriteria: The method is explicit and repeatable: scales, criteria, rating rules, confidence levels and treatment thresholds are stated rather than implied.
Findings are evidence-based. At least some conclusions rest on technique-based testing, and each finding cites the test performed, the artefact examined and the date.

The assessment names Vanguard's actual risks, including payments disruption, customer data exposure through cloud identity sprawl, third-party dependency and unsupported technology, rather than a catalogue of generic cyber threats.
The inventory reconciliation is honest about gaps and does not present an aspirational asset list as if it were verified.
Risk reasoning is sound: likelihood and impact are argued from the business context, including the regulatory consequence and the customer impact, and the ratings are defensible under challenge.
Existing risk acceptances are surfaced and challenged where the assessment finds them invalid, rather than silently re-rating risks that the business has already accepted.
The treatment plan distinguishes risk reduction, risk avoidance, risk transfer and acceptance, states cost and dependency, and does not present monitoring as remediation.
Governance findings on the three lines model and second line independence are included rather than treated as out of scope.
The report states residual risk clearly, including the risks that remain above appetite after the recommended treatment, and identifies the decisions the board must take.
The board presentation is decision-oriented and free of technical detail that a non-executive director cannot use.
items.modelSolution:
The first decision is what the assessment is for. Vanguard has three plausible objectives and they produce different reports: a regulatory readiness exercise, a security posture improvement programme, or an input to the enterprise risk process. The CRO's stated need, a single reconciled enterprise cyber risk view reporting monthly, makes the third the primary objective, with regulatory readiness as a constraint and posture improvement as a consequence rather than the goal. That framing should be stated up front in the method document, because it determines what gets rated and how.

Before any testing, deal with inventory. In every bank of this shape the CMDB, the network drawings and the cloud configuration exports disagree, and the assessment's credibility depends on which one you treat as truth. The answer is to treat all three as evidence, reconcile them mechanically, and publish the disagreement as a finding. If a server appears in the CMDB but not in the cloud export, that is either shadow IT or stale records, and either way it is out of the control set the CISO believes exists. Doing this properly will produce a residual inventory with confidence ratings: high confidence where two sources agree, medium where one source and a scan corroborate, low where only documentation exists. Publishing the confidence ratings is what stops the bank overstating its coverage to the regulator.

The method should combine three lenses rather than picking one. A governance and organisational assessment covers the three lines model, second line independence, risk appetite translation into control thresholds, and committee reporting quality. A control effectiveness assessment tests a defined sample with technique rather than reading policy. A threat-led assessment models realistic attack paths for the two scenarios that matter to this bank. The third lens is what most assessments omit and what makes the output credible to a bank board, because it expresses control gaps as business exposure rather than as a percentage of controls operating.

For control testing, select a sample that is genuinely representative of the risk and of the estate rather than a convenience sample. For a bank of this size a defensible minimum covers privileged access recertification on the core banking platform, cloud IAM privilege sprawl across all three accounts, log coverage and retention on the payments hub, branch WAN segmentation and the patching window for internet-facing systems, offboarding process for a sample of leavers including the departed employee in the complaint, and third-party remote access. Test technique should be explicit: pull the recertification files and check that signatures correspond to the period, check whether reviewers were members of the team that provisioned the access, check whether exceptions exist without expiry, and sample the exception population. If a control claims to operate at 95 percent but the underlying population shows a systematic exclusion of the highest-privilege accounts, the control is not operating, and you need to say so with the numbers.

Two attack paths make the point to the board. The first, internet-facing credential compromise against internet banking: entry through a compromised privileged third-party support account, privilege escalation inside the identity layer where cloud roles are broad and the path to the customer profile store is short, and detection failing because the identity telemetry is not correlated with the payments telemetry. Break points along that path are specific controls. The second, insider: a departed employee whose access was not fully removed, joined by log retention that makes retrospective investigation impossible. This is where the anonymous complaint becomes more than an HR process failure, because the same configuration prevents the bank from proving what did or did not happen.

Reconciling with the enterprise risk register is where a good assessment becomes an organisational product. Map every significant finding to the 118 existing risks. Where a finding lands on a risk that the business has already accepted, do not silently re-rate it, because that destroys trust. Instead, present it as a challenge to an existing acceptance, with the specific reason the acceptance is no longer valid: the risk was accepted in 2024 on the basis that the data warehouse was isolated, and it is no longer isolated. Several of the six above-appetite risks will turn out to be cyber risks that no business head owns knowingly, which is the finding the CRO actually needs.

Treatment options need discipline about the difference between reducing and shifting exposure. Migrating a workload to the cloud without fixing identity design and logging does not reduce risk, it relocates it and removes the local physical controls the bank relied on. Transfer through a cyber insurance policy is worth stating explicitly, but the first thing to check is whether exclusions cover the dominant scenario. Preventive and detective controls should be sequenced so that detective capability exists before a preventive control is removed, otherwise the bank has a period of lower cost and lower detection.

For the board, the report should state residual risk after treatment, not before, and name the risks that remain above appetite and require an explicit board decision. Monthly reporting to the CRO should be a single page per risk with movement since last month, so that the view is genuinely sustainable. Where the assessment and the CISO disagree on a rating, record the disagreement and the reason in the paper rather than splitting the difference, because a risk committee can adjudicate an argument and cannot adjudicate a blended number.
items.managementFeedback:
This is the assessment I asked for and I want to be clear that you delivered something quite different from what I expected. I expected a security posture scorecard with a percentage and a colour. You delivered a reconciled view that I can take to the enterprise risk committee and that the business heads can act on. The inventory reconciliation with confidence ratings was particularly useful, because it showed the CRO's new CRO has been making decisions on a view of the estate that was 15 percent wrong.

Three things I am pushing back on. First, the attack path work. It is well evidenced and it is the part of the report that will get read by the board, but it currently describes technical break points without quantifying business exposure. If a path to the payments hub is presented only as a path, I will be asked what it costs. Second, the treatment plan leans heavily on migration to the cloud, and the cloud is where two of our six above-appetite risks already sit. Migration without identity and logging remediation is relocation, not risk reduction, and I need that distinction stated in a way the CTO will accept rather than in a footnote. Third, you have not challenged the existing risk acceptances hard enough. Where a business head accepted a risk in 2024 on the basis of a state that no longer exists, your job is to say so directly and put the challenge on record. I will back you when you do, and it will be uncomfortable for one or two of the heads.

What I found genuinely good: the offboarding and log retention analysis ties directly to the complaint we received, which is exactly the kind of evidence that changes an organisation's behaviour rather than just satisfying an audit. And the monthly one-page-per-risk format is designed to survive contact with a busy CRO, which is more than I can say for the previous quarterly deck.

If you want to go further, the next step is a tabletop on the insider scenario with the actual people from the SOC, HR and internal audit. If the answer under pressure is still 'we would check the logs', then we have a capability gap, and I would rather know that in a room than in a regulatory examination.

items.title: Perform an NIST CSF 2.0 gap assessment and build the roadmap
items.background: Sarvam Industries Ltd. is a fictional listed manufacturer of consumer electronics and industrial components, with 14,000 employees across 22 plants in India and contract operations in three other countries. It sells to global original equipment manufacturers who increasingly write supplier security requirements into their standard purchasing terms, and it holds consumer and employee data for loyalty, warranty, warranty-claim and employee payroll purposes. The IT estate is a mixture of an on-premises ERP and plant manufacturing execution system, three cloud accounts across two hyperscalers, a customer-facing warranty portal that was migrated to the cloud in the last eighteen months, and an operational technology layer of roughly 4,000 industrial devices running across the plants with a separate network segment that is monitored but not inventoried. Sarvam is subject to the Indian Digital Personal Data Protection Act and rules, the CERT-In directions on incident reporting, and the listing governance requirements of the securities regulator, which require a board-approved risk management framework and a periodic risk disclosure. A global OEM customer has written NIST CSF 2.0 Tier 2 alignment with evidence of current function implementation into its next purchasing agreement, and a second customer has asked for a supply chain risk management programme with contractual reporting of the firm's own sub-tier suppliers. Two years ago a consultant ran a vulnerability scan across the corporate estate and produced 412 raw findings that nobody has been able to translate into business risk, and the executive committee has received conflicting reports from the CISO, the plant operations team and the internal audit function about the real exposure. The CFO has asked for a single gap assessment and a costed three-year roadmap that the board can approve in one sitting.
items.scope: In scope: the corporate IT environment including ERP, HR and payroll, the customer warranty portal, the three cloud accounts and the identity and network services supporting them, and the governance layers of CSF 2.0 Govern that Sarvam either has or does not have. In scope is also the supplier ecosystem that Sarvam depends on for components, logistics and outsourced IT, to the depth needed to assess the CSF 2.0 supply chain functions. Out of scope is a full assessment of operational technology and industrial control system security, which is covered by a separate OT assessment with an ICS profile; only the boundary and dependency from IT to OT is assessed here. Out of scope is the substantive safety and process control risk of manufacturing, product cybersecurity of Sarvam-designed hardware, and detailed privacy compliance, which sits with the DPO and legal. Out of scope is any assessment of the accuracy of financial reporting, which is owned by the statutory auditor.
objectives: Build a CSF 2.0 gap assessment grounded in current state evidence, using the six functions and the organisational tiers, rather than a maturity score derived from policy review alone.
Establish Sarvam's Tier position by function and justify it against the business case, the customer contractual requirement and the regulatory context.
Translate the 412 unprioritised scan findings into a small set of business-relevant exposures with a defensible prioritisation method.
Assess the CSF 2.0 Govern functions in detail, since these are the functions most often skipped and the ones that determine whether anything else is sustainable.
Assess the Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management functions, including Sarvam's own supplier tiers and the way supplier risk is contractually managed.
Produce a current state and target state profile for each function and subcategory, with a gap rationale and a source of evidence for each judgement.
Build a three-year costed roadmap sequenced by dependency and by risk reduction, with owners, quick wins and the business case per tranche.
Deliver an executive and board-level story that connects the roadmap to the customer contract, the regulatory position and the cost of the alternatives.
Define the ongoing measurement approach, including the current state profile refresh cycle, so the programme does not decay into a one-off project.
startingInformation: Sarvam has 14,000 employees and 22 plants; 38 percent of revenue comes from three OEM customers whose purchasing terms now include cybersecurity requirements.
The CISO is nine months into the role and inherited a team of 22 with no defined ownership of third-party risk; third-party risk was absorbed by procurement after a reorganisation.
There is no documented inventory of the OT estate. The estimate is roughly 4,000 industrial devices and the plant security manager maintains a spreadsheet covering only 9 of the 22 plants.

The warranty portal was migrated to a public cloud 18 months ago. The team has since grown from 6 to 19 cloud accounts across two hyperscalers with no landing zone, no organisation-wide logging and no evidence of a single cloud access review.

A 2024 consultant vulnerability scan produced 412 findings. 61 have been remediated, 351 remain, and there is no agreed risk acceptance or treatment plan for them. The CISO cannot tell the board which of them matter.

A second consultant report in 2025 rated Sarvam against CSF 1.1 and concluded Tier 2 for Identify and Protect, but the underlying evidence was a set of interviews and 26 policy documents, and two of the ratings have since been challenged by internal audit.
Sarvam has an enterprise risk register maintained by the CFO's team with 84 risks; only three reference cybersecurity, and there is no linkage between the risk register and the security programme.

The listed-company governance rules require a board-approved risk management framework, a risk management committee and a periodic risk disclosure; a cyber risk committee exists but meets quarterly with minutes that record attendance only.

The OEM customer's purchasing agreement requires current state and target state profiles aligned to CSF 2.0, evidence of function implementation for two Tier 2 functions, and a named customer security contact within 30 days of the contract's next revision date.
Budget: 6 crore rupees has been provisionally set aside for the first year of the roadmap, with the CFO requiring a tranche-by-tranche release and a clear return for each tranche.
The CISO reports to the CIO, who reports to the CFO. The board risk committee has asked to see the assessment directly because of a shareholder question about a ransomware event at a peer company.
Internal audit will independently validate the assessment, and its head has told the CISO in advance that any rating unsupported by evidence will be reported as a finding.
activities: Confirm the assessment scope, the in-scope environments, the exclusions and the criteria sources, including the OEM contract, the listing governance rules, the data protection obligations and the CERT-In directions.
Establish the current state evidence base: gather the CSF 2.0 subcategory-level evidence available today, record where it is absent and rate the confidence of each judgement.
Interview the six function owners and the key control owners to understand how each function actually operates day to day, and reconcile interview answers against documentary evidence.

Perform the Govern function assessment in detail, covering organisational context, roles and responsibilities, risk management strategy, legal and regulatory requirements, information sharing and supply chain.
Assess identity and access across the 19 cloud accounts and the on-premises estate, including privileged access, service accounts, joiner-mover-leaver and access recertification.
Assess asset management and inventory, specifically the absence of an OT inventory, and document the IT-to-OT boundary and the dependencies that cross it.
Run and interpret a prioritisation exercise on the 412 outstanding scan findings, converting technical severity into business-relevant exposure using asset criticality and data classification.
Assess protective technology coverage including network segmentation, encryption, backup and recovery, and the actual restoration evidence rather than the backup policy.
Assess detection and response capability with the SOC and the incident response team, including whether OT and IT telemetry are correlated and how the CERT-In six-hour reporting obligation is met.
Perform the Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management assessment, mapping Sarvam's critical suppliers and sub-tier dependencies and reviewing the contractual security clauses in place.
Establish and defend Sarvam's Tier position function by function, with the justification recorded in the current state profile.
Build the target state profile per function and subcategory, then translate the gaps into a three-year roadmap with tranches, dependencies, owners and indicative cost.
Validate the assessment and roadmap with the CISO, the CFO, the risk committee and internal audit, and re-rate any judgement that cannot be evidenced.
Present the roadmap to the board risk committee with the business case, the contractual driver and the measurement approach, and capture the decisions and funding tranches approved.
deliverables: CSF 2.0 assessment scope, criteria and method statement with confidence ratings for each judgement
Current state profile for all six functions and their subcategories, with sources of evidence and explicit not-assessed markings
Tier position assessment by function with justification against business case, customer contract and regulatory context
Detailed CSF 2.0 Govern function assessment with gaps in organisational context, roles, legal requirements and supply chain
Prioritised remediation backlog that reconciles the 412 outstanding scan findings into business-relevant exposures
Cybersecurity supply chain risk assessment with critical supplier map and contractual clause review
Target state profile per function and a three-year costed roadmap with tranches, dependencies and owners
Board paper and risk committee presentation with the business case, decision requests and measurement approach
Measurement framework defining the current state refresh cycle, metrics and reporting cadence
evaluationCriteria: Each current state judgement is tied to a named evidence source or explicitly marked as not assessed with a confidence rating. Unsupported ratings are treated as a material weakness.

The gap analysis reaches into the Govern and Supply Chain functions in genuine depth rather than treating them as documentary exercises, which is where CSF 2.0 differs from CSF 1.1 and where most assessments stop short.
The 412 scan findings are converted into a small, defensible, prioritised set with a stated prioritisation logic that combines technical severity, asset criticality and data exposure.
The Tier position argument is grounded in the customer contractual requirement and the business case, not simply in a scoring model, and the reasoning survives a challenge from the CISO.
The roadmap is sequenced by dependency and risk reduction rather than by function, includes quick wins in the first ninety days, and each tranche has an owner and a cost.
The business case is expressed in terms the CFO and board act on: contract value at risk, exposure reduction and the cost of doing nothing, with assumptions stated.
Supply chain assessment addresses Sarvam's own suppliers and sub-tier dependencies, and reviews whether contractual clauses exist to obtain the evidence the assessment assumed it had.
The OT boundary is handled honestly, with the inventory gap named as a finding rather than smoothed over, and the recommendation to separately assess OT using an ICS profile is justified.
The measurement approach is specified in operational terms: refresh cycle, metrics, thresholds, owners and where the output goes.
The board paper is written for non-technical directors and makes the decision requests explicit rather than describing the assessment.
items.modelSolution:
Start by being precise about what CSF 2.0 is for in this business, because that determines the shape of the deliverable. CSF 2.0 is not a certification scheme and it is not a control catalogue; it is an organising framework for talking about cybersecurity outcomes. Sarvam's three real drivers are an OEM customer who will put Tier 2 evidence into a purchasing agreement, a listed-company governance obligation to run a board-approved risk management framework, and a genuine security problem in a cloud sprawl and an un-inventoried OT estate. The assessment should therefore serve three functions at once: an evidence base for the customer contract, a defensible board narrative, and a costed remediation plan. Write that purpose down in the method statement, because a CSF assessment that cannot say what decision it supports will produce a tier rating nobody acts on.

CSF 2.0's real structural change from 1.1 is the addition of Govern and the explicit elevation of supply chain. A lot of assessors treat Govern as an organisational preamble and rush to the Protect and Detect functions, where the scanning data is. That would be a mistake here, because Sarvam's most consequential gaps are exactly in Govern: there is no defined third-party risk ownership, the risk committee's minutes record attendance rather than decisions, the risk register has only three cyber risks, and legal and regulatory requirements are not translated into internal requirements anywhere. CSF 2.0 also reframes cybersecurity risk management so it is governed as an enterprise concern with roles and responsibilities explicitly named, which is a direct hit on Sarvam's governance weakness.

The evidence base must be built before the rating. For each subcategory, gather what exists and record what does not, with a confidence rating. Where the only source is an interview, mark it as such; where the source is a system export or a tested configuration, say so. Internal audit has already signalled that it will report unsupported ratings as findings, so the discipline is not optional. Where an owner asserts a function is implemented and no artefact exists, record the gap rather than the assertion. A current state profile with a lot of not-assessed markings and high confidence in a handful of areas is far more useful to the board than a uniformly green profile that cannot be defended.

Tier position needs to be argued, not computed. CSF 2.0 tiers describe the sophistication of the risk management processes in place, not the quality of the outcome. Sarvam should realistically be assessed at Tier 1 for several functions, Tier 2 for a couple where the new CISO has genuinely built something, and partial for others. The customer contract requires evidence for two specific Tier 2 functions, which is a strong argument for prioritising those two functions regardless of where the assessment lands overall. That is the right trade-off to make and to state: meet the contractual obligation in the two named functions, and treat the rest as a sequenced improvement programme.

The 412 scan findings are where most assessments drown. Build a prioritisation logic that combines technical severity with asset criticality and data sensitivity, and then convert findings into a small set of exposures a board can act on. An unpatched print server on a plant network segment is not a board-level exposure; an unpatched internet-facing VPN concentrator that terminates retail loyalty traffic with stored credentials is. Show the mechanics of the reduction so the CISO can defend it to the CTO, and be honest that reduction comes partly from accepting risk in areas where the OT network is intentionally segmented. That acceptance needs documenting and a compensating control, not hiding.

Supply chain is the second area that deserves real effort. Map the critical suppliers by what they can do to Sarvam, which means component suppliers, the logistics providers who handle outbound data, and the outsourced IT providers who hold privileged access. Then do the part that most assessments omit: check whether the contracts actually give Sarvam the right to obtain the evidence the assessment has been assuming. If the terms with a critical outsourced IT provider contain no audit right and no security schedule, then no amount of assessment effort produces assurance, and the correct recommendation is a contract change, which is a procurement action rather than a security action. That insight is often the most valuable output of the whole exercise.

On OT, resist the temptation to score it in CSF 2.0's IT-centric subcategories. Sarvam's operational technology needs a separate assessment using the ICS profile, and the CSF 2.0 assessment should record the boundary: what the IT environment can reach into OT, what shared services exist, whether the segmentation is enforced or merely documented, and whether plant incident response knows how to escalate. The missing inventory is itself a finding and it should be named as one in the board paper.

Build the target state and roadmap together, otherwise it becomes a wish list. Sequence by dependency: identity and inventory before detection engineering, detection before removal of compensating controls, monitoring and evidence before the customer audit. Tranche one, within ninety days, should be the things that are cheap and unlock later work: ownership and governance decisions, a federated inventory baseline, access recertification for privileged cloud identities, closure of the scan backlog triage, and the measurement baseline. Tranche two builds the operational capability. Tranche three extends to supply chain, OT integration and auditability of the programme itself. Each tranche gets a cost, an owner and a short statement of what risk it removes, so the CFO can release funding against evidence of progress rather than against a plan.

The business case should be explicit. Name the contract value exposed to the OEM requirement, the fact that the peer ransomware event has already moved the board's sensitivity, and the regulatory reporting obligation that makes detection latency a compliance issue rather than only an operational one. Then state the cost of doing nothing as the alternative scenario, because the board will make that comparison regardless of whether you do.

Finally, define the refresh cycle. CSF 2.0 is explicit that the current state profile is a point-in-time view and should be refreshed, typically annually or on material change. Set the refresh cadence, the metric set, the thresholds that trigger escalation, and where the output goes. A framework assessment with no refresh mechanism becomes an artefact nobody reads by the third quarter.
items.managementFeedback:
You have done something I did not expect from a first assessment, which is to be honest about what you could not assess. Three functions came back with low confidence and a substantial not-assessed population, and I would have said that was a failure. In fact it is the most credible thing in the pack, because it tells us exactly where we are blind. The internal audit head has separately told me that your confidence ratings are the first thing she has been able to rely on when she reviews our security material.

Where I am uncomfortable is the roadmap. Tranche one is sensible and I am happy to fund it. Tranche three contains an OT assessment, supplier contract remediation and auditability of the programme, and the indicative cost makes me wince, particularly the supplier contract piece, because I know what legal will do with it. I need you to come back with the contractual exposure quantified. If it turns out that a failed OEM audit costs us the contract, that is a number I can act on. If it does not, then the honest answer may be that the supplier work belongs in procurement's plan with our support rather than in the security budget, and I would rather hear that from you than discover it later.

The other pushback is the tier position. You have rated several functions at Tier 1, which I know the CISO is unhappy about, and I understand why, but I need the argument presented so that it protects the bank rather than flattering the CISO. Say clearly which two functions will be evidenced at Tier 2 for the OEM, by when, and how we will know. If the answer is that we can do it inside tranche two, then the tier argument becomes a sequencing argument and the profile ratings become a secondary issue.

What would make me take this to the board with confidence: the decision requests. Right now the paper describes the assessment well and asks the board to note it. I need three decisions with cost attached, a deadline, and a named owner for each. That is what turns a good assessment into a funded programme.

items.title: Conduct an internal IT general controls audit
items.background: Coastal Health Group is a fictional 2,400-bed hospital group operating six hospitals and fourteen clinics across three states, with about 9,000 employees including 3,100 clinical staff and a shared services centre of 420 people in Chennai. Two smaller community hospitals were acquired in the last two years and their finance and clinical systems were never integrated, so the group now runs four distinct patient administration systems, three general ledgers and a patchwork of departmental applications for pharmacy, laboratory and imaging. The statutory auditor of the group has raised a query in the current year on whether reliance can be placed on automated controls in the revenue cycle, and the audit committee has asked internal audit to provide assurance over the IT general control environment before the financial close rather than after it. A new CFO joined eight months ago and has inherited a decentralised IT function of 260 people, most of whom report to site administrators rather than to a group function, and a system landscape where clinical systems, the ERP, payroll and the revenue cycle all share an Active Directory domain in a single flat trust. Six months ago one hospital was taken offline for eleven hours by a ransomware payload that entered through a supplier-maintained radiology PACS server with shared local administrator credentials, and the recovery was completed by restoring backups without any documented test of the restore point or of the clinical data integrity of the restored systems. A donor organisation that funds the group's paediatric programme has asked for an independent controls report covering the systems that record donor-funded activity. The chief audit executive reports functionally to the audit committee and administratively to the CFO, which is about to become a point of tension when the audit reaches the systems the CFO's own team operates.
items.scope: In scope: the IT general controls over all applications and systems that feed the financial statements and the regulatory reporting of the group, namely the general ledger, patient administration and revenue cycle systems, payroll, the fixed asset register, procurement and pharmacy inventory, the donor management system, and the interfaces and reports that flow between them. Also in scope are the infrastructure supporting those applications, the group Active Directory domain and identity services, change management over production systems, computer operations including backup and restore, and physical and logical access to the data centres and server rooms, including third-party and vendor access. Out of scope is the design and operation of clinical safety controls and medical device management, which belong to the clinical governance function, although the audit notes where information security failures have clinical consequences. Out of scope is substantive testing of revenue, expenditure and payroll balances, which is the statutory auditor's work, and out of scope is the clinical systems' data quality and the content of medical records. The audit is a controls audit, not a penetration test and not a clinical process review.
objectives: Define the audit objectives, the systems in the financial reporting boundary and the IT general control categories to be tested, with clear reliance objectives for the statutory auditor.
Establish the audit universe of applications, interfaces and infrastructure that support the financial reporting boundary, including the four patient administration systems.
Test access to programs and data, including joiner-mover-leaver, privileged access, service accounts and vendor access, and rate the control design and operating effectiveness.
Test program change management, including emergency changes, across ERP, revenue cycle and clinical-adjacent financial systems.
Test computer operations including job scheduling, batch interfaces, backup, restore testing and incident recovery against the eleven-hour ransomware event.
Assess whether the four unintegrated systems and the flat domain trust create a control dependency risk that the group's risk register does not capture.
Evaluate the independence and reporting line of internal audit, and design the escalation path for findings that implicate the CFO's own function.
Deliver findings that distinguish control deficiency from control weakness from significant deficiency, with severity calibrated using the actual financial and clinical exposure.
Produce a management action plan with owners, dates and root causes, and provide the committee with an unfiltered view of the control environment's maturity.
startingInformation: The group has four patient administration systems, three general ledgers, 27 departmental applications and more than 90 interfaces feeding the consolidated reporting used by the statutory auditor.

IT is decentralised: 260 IT staff across six hospitals and the Chennai shared services centre, with only three enterprise-level roles (network, server, service desk) and the remainder reporting to site IT managers.
There is a single Active Directory domain for the entire group, with 6,400 user accounts and a flat trust model between the hospital networks.

The ransomware event six months ago: entry via a supplier-maintained PACS server with shared local administrator credentials, 11 hours of downtime at one hospital, restoration from backups, and no documented test of the restore point or of the integrity of the restored clinical records.

Backup for the group is nightly and full for the ERP and the revenue cycle, but the four patient administration systems and two of the three general ledgers are on a different schedule, and the group has never performed a documented end-to-end restore test with clinical users.

The statutory auditor's current-year query on automated controls in the revenue cycle is unresolved and the audit committee has asked internal audit to report by the next committee meeting, 11 weeks away.
The audit committee approved an internal audit plan of 14 audits for the year, of which this is one; 6 are complete, 3 are in field, and 5 are scheduled.

Internal audit has 18 staff including 4 IT auditors. The group has no ITGC specialist on the team and previously outsourced this work to a firm whose deliverable was a report of 60 findings with no severity calibration.
The CISO role does not exist. Information security sits under the IT operations head, who also owns the infrastructure that is the subject of this audit.
A draft audit finding register from the previous outsourced ITGC work contains 60 findings, 44 of which remain marked open, with an average age of 22 months.
The donor organisation requires a controls report covering systems recording donor-funded activity within 120 days, for a grant worth 3 crore rupees per year.

Policy exists for access management, change management, backup and vendor access, with a documented 30-day leaver deprovisioning SLA; the IT helpdesk system records 63 breaches of that SLA in the last 12 months.
activities: Obtain and validate the audit objectives with the audit committee and the statutory auditor, and agree the reliance framework and the intended reliance on ITGCs in the audit of financial statements.
Define the financial reporting boundary and the audit universe of applications, interfaces and infrastructure, and reconcile the group application register to the finance team's reporting inventory.
Review prior audit findings, specifically the 44 open items from the outsourced ITGC report, and assess the root cause of the 22-month average age of open items.
Perform walkthroughs of the access, change and computer operations controls in each of the six hospitals and in shared services, following the transaction from initiation to recording.

Test application access to programs and data across the ERP, revenue cycle and payroll, including user provisioning, role design, leaver deprovisioning, privileged access, service accounts and vendor accounts.

Test program change management for standard, normal and emergency changes across the ERP and revenue cycle, including testing the ability to segregate developers from production, and cover the clinical-adjacent systems.

Test computer operations including job and interface scheduling, batch failure handling and restart, backup completeness, off-site copy retention and the evidence of a genuine end-to-end restore test.

Evaluate the design of the flat domain trust and the four unintegrated systems, assess whether they create a control dependency for other sites, and determine whether this is captured in the group risk register.
Re-perform the eleven-hour ransomware recovery on a sample of non-production data to test whether the documented recovery is achievable and whether clinical data integrity can be demonstrated.

Perform a service organisation review of the radiology PACS and other critical vendor-managed systems, covering the shared credential finding, contractual right to access evidence and third-party assurance reports.
Evaluate the internal audit independence question, agree the escalation route with the audit committee chair for findings implicating the CFO's function, and put the arrangement on record.
Synthesise findings, calibrate severity against the actual financial, regulatory and clinical exposure, draft the report and discuss all findings with management before issuing.
Report to the audit committee, obtain management's response and action plan with owners and dates, and follow up the implementation.
deliverables: Audit objectives, reliance statement and agreed scope memorandum with the audit committee and statutory auditor
Financial reporting boundary document and reconciled audit universe of applications, interfaces and infrastructure
Prior findings status report covering the 44 open items, with root cause analysis of why items aged to 22 months
Control testing workpapers for access, change management and computer operations across six hospitals and shared services
Testing summary for joiner-mover-leaver, privileged access, service accounts and vendor access, including the leaver SLA breach analysis
Restore and recovery test report based on a re-performed end-to-end restoration, with clinical data integrity observations
Third-party and service organisation review of vendor-managed clinical and financial systems
Findings report with severity calibration, root causes and a management action plan with owners and dates
Audit committee report and presentation with the unfiltered view of control environment maturity and the independence arrangement
evaluationCriteria: The audit is driven by the reporting boundary and reliance objectives rather than by a generic ITGC checklist, and the boundary reconciliation exposes discrepancies in the group's own application inventory.
Testing is performed with technique. Walkthroughs are used to establish design and then samples are traced to evidence, not policy statements quoted as evidence of operation.

Findings are severity-calibrated with reference to actual financial, regulatory and clinical exposure, and the report distinguishes control deficiency, control weakness and significant deficiency rather than listing all findings as high.
The 44 open prior findings are addressed head on. Either they are closed with evidence, or the report states why they remain open and what the aggregate effect on the control environment is.

The flat domain trust and the four unintegrated systems are analysed for control dependency across sites, and the conclusion is routed into the group risk register rather than living only in the audit report.
The ransomware recovery is tested rather than accepted, and the report distinguishes a recovery plan that exists from a recovery capability that has been proven.

Vendor-managed systems are examined with the same rigour as internally operated ones, including contractual access rights, and the shared administrator credential finding is pursued to its root cause in the vendor's processes.

The internal audit independence issue is handled with candour and in the right forum, with a documented escalation path for findings that implicate the CFO's function, and the report does not soften the conclusion to protect the relationship.
The action plan names owners with the authority to fix, contains dates that are realistic, and includes root causes rather than restating the control objective.
The committee report is honest about the overall state of the environment and does not present a partial improvement as a mature control environment.
items.modelSolution:
The most important thing this audit has to do is earn the label that the previous outsourced engagement did not deserve, so the report and its structure need to be built around what the audit committee and the statutory auditor actually asked for. The committee asked for confidence over the revenue cycle automation before the financial close. The statutory auditor asked whether reliance can be placed on automated controls. Both are reliance questions, so the audit is not a general IT maturity review. It starts with the financial reporting boundary, and the boundary is the hard part, because this group genuinely does not know what it has.

Before testing anything, reconcile. There is a group application register, the finance team's reporting inventory and the infrastructure asset list, and they will not agree. Four patient administration systems, three general ledgers and ninety interfaces is not a large estate, but it is a fragmented one, and the interfaces are where the controls live. Build the universe by tracing which systems actually feed the consolidated numbers the auditor examines, and document every interface by direction, frequency, and what happens on failure. This reconciliation is itself a reportable finding, because if the group's own inventory cannot be reconciled with the finance inventory, the auditor's reliance question cannot be answered either, and that is the message the audit committee needs to hear first.

Then handle the 44 open prior findings properly, because the average age of 22 months is the single most damning number available and it is a governance failure as much as a technical one. Either the findings were wrong, the remediation did not work, the accountability was not assigned, or nobody was tracking. Determine which by testing a sample against current state rather than by reading the closure notes. The likely answer is that the prior findings were largely generic, had no owner beyond the IT operations head, and were never escalated because the report was delivered to an IT management meeting rather than to the audit committee. That is the root cause worth writing, and it changes how every finding in this report should be handled.

Walkthroughs come next, at each of the six hospitals, because the control that matters may be designed properly in the shared services centre and operated differently in a site. Follow one transaction from initiation to recording for a patient charge, a payroll change and a purchase order. Design is assessed from the walkthrough and operating effectiveness from the sample. The 63 breaches of the 30-day leaver deprovisioning SLA recorded in the helpdesk system are directly relevant, so use them as the population for leaver testing rather than a sample of convenience: for a sample of leavers, determine the actual date of separation, the date access was removed and the date of the leaver report, and calculate the lag for each. The SLA breaches become an exception population with a measured distribution, which is far harder for management to dismiss than an auditor's own sample of five.

Change management is where hospital environments usually fail, because clinical availability creates legitimate emergency changes and the emergency label becomes a loophole. Test the classification of changes, the approval evidence for emergency changes after the fact, whether testing occurred before promotion to production, and whether segregation of duties holds for the people who both develop and promote. Include the clinical-adjacent financial systems, because the revenue cycle and pharmacy inventory interfaces change in ways that affect reported numbers even when the change looks clinical.

Computer operations needs a real restore test. The ransomware recovery is the obvious reason. Rather than re-asking IT whether the backups work, re-perform the recovery on a representative sample using the documented procedure and record the elapsed time, the steps that required improvisation, the point at which the procedure failed and the point at which clinical users could work. Then assess the second question the group has never asked: whether the restored clinical data was consistent. Restoring data from a point in time and then catching up transactions by hand is exactly where clinical records become unreliable, and in a teaching hospital that becomes a patient safety issue that is not the audit's remit but is squarely within its duty to escalate. The deliverable is a statement of what the recovery capability actually is, which is likely a capability of some hours with significant improvisation, rather than the eleven-hour figure in the incident record.

The flat domain trust is the structural risk and needs careful, proportionate analysis. A single domain across six hospitals with 6,400 accounts means one compromised local administrator account at any site can attempt access elsewhere, whether or not it succeeds. The audit should not assert that it has succeeded, and it should not ignore the dependency. Test whether it does succeed in the sites that were not affected, determine what the actual compensating controls are, and then take the finding to the group risk register, because a single-trust architecture across a hospital group is a group-level risk that no site risk register owns. In the same vein, note the absence of a CISO and the fact that information security sits under the IT operations head who owns the very infrastructure being audited, which is a structural conflict of interest that the committee should address as part of the governance response.

Vendor-managed systems deserve equal scrutiny, particularly the radiology PACS supplier whose shared local administrator credentials were the entry point. The questions are specific: is the credential still shared, is it rotated, is there individual accountability, what does the contract say about access and audit rights, and what assurance evidence does the supplier provide about its own controls. A shared administrator account on a supplier-maintained server is a root cause, not an incident, and the audit should name it as such in the root cause section and require closure with evidence.

The independence issue must be handled directly and in the right forum. The chief audit executive reports administratively to the CFO while auditing systems operated by the CFO's function. The audit committee chair should be told this in a private session before the report is issued, the arrangement should be documented, and the report should state plainly which findings implicate the CFO's function and how they were handled. Softening them would be both wrong and, given that the audit committee is a sophisticated customer, obvious.

Finally, calibrate severity against exposure rather than against control language. A failed deprovisioning SLA in a hospital where shared workstations exist in clinical bays has a genuinely different consequence from a failed one in an office, and the difference should be reflected in severity. Group findings by root cause, because the headline is rarely one failed control but one broken process repeated, and the committee's decision is about the process. The action plan must name owners who have the authority to act and dates that are credible, and it should distinguish the actions required for the statutory audit from the actions that materially improve the environment.
items.managementFeedback:
The report reads like an audit rather than a list, and I can see the difference between it and the last one immediately. The single most valuable thing in it is the root cause analysis of the 44 open findings.
