I was not aware that the closure notes were evidence-free and that the findings had been routed to an IT management meeting instead of this committee. That is on me and on my team, and it needs correcting.

Two areas where I want more. First, the restore test. Your finding that the eleven-hour recovery depended on improvisation, and that restored clinical data integrity was never demonstrated, is the most serious thing in the pack and it is currently written in language that reads as a caution. I want it written plainly: we do not know that we can recover our clinical systems to a known-good state within a business-acceptable window, and we do not know that the data we restore is complete. That needs to be a named risk owned by a named executive with a date, not an audit observation. I have already told the COO.

Second, the shared vendor administrator credential. You identified it as a root cause and that is right, but the action sits with the supplier, and suppliers do not respond to audit findings. If you want this closed, you will need to tell the procurement team that our contract does not give us the access rights we need, and that the closure condition is contractual, not technical. Take me with you when you have that conversation, because I will get the renegotiation scheduled.

On the independence point: you handled it correctly and I appreciate that you did not soften the findings that touch my team. I would rather have that discomfort now than an adverse finding from the committee later. Continue to report to the chair on it, and I will not pressure you.

What would make me recommend you for the next step: the report is strong on diagnosis and the management action plan is still the weak part. Several of the dates I have been given are ones I cannot hold my teams to, because the root cause sits in shared services and shared services has no single accountable owner. If you can help me design one, I will fund it.

items.title: Develop a third-party risk management programme
items.background: Vanguard Financial Services Ltd. is a fictional 5,000-employee universal bank based in Mumbai with 640 branches, a 180-person IT operations team, a 24x7 security operations centre and a data centre in Chennai, alongside retail and corporate banking platforms and a domestic payments hub. The bank depends on a large and fast-growing set of external parties: the integrator that supports its core banking platform, the payment aggregator through which most merchant acquiring flows, the primary cloud provider that hosts an increasing share of customer workloads, the screening and monitoring vendors behind its financial crime controls, the credit bureau, an ATM managed services operator, and a business process outsourcer with 900 staff handling customer service and collections from a single site. Third-party risk has never been owned by a single function. Procurement owns contracts, information security owns technology assessments, operational risk owns vendor risk in the enterprise register, and the business owns the relationship, and each keeps its own records. A supplier assurance review last year produced 90 open findings across 40 vendors with no common severity model and no single tracker. Twelve weeks ago the payments aggregator failed an information security assessment with a critical finding around segregation of the merchant onboarding data, and the business unit that owns the relationship accepted it verbally. In the same quarter a KYC screening vendor announced it had moved customer identity data to a new sub-processor in another country without notifying the bank, which was discovered only because the bank's data protection officer noticed a change in the vendor's published sub-processor register. The regulator's directions require the board to approve a third-party risk management policy, to identify and manage the risks arising from outsourced activities, and to have a comprehensive register of third-party relationships; the bank currently has three disconnected registers and no tiering model. The chief risk officer wants a programme that will stand up to examination while the chief information security officer wants it to stop being a document exercise.
items.scope: In scope: all third-party relationships that support the bank's business processes, including technology and cloud providers, payment and settlement service providers, financial crime screening and monitoring vendors, credit information bureaus, managed ATM and cash logistics operators, business process outsourcers including offshore service operations, and the professional advisers and audit firms the bank appoints. In scope is the full lifecycle from business need and due diligence through contracting, onboarding, ongoing monitoring, offboarding and exit, including the bank's obligations to oversee service providers as if they were the bank's own. Also in scope is the register and the risk classification of third parties. Out of scope is procurement policy and commercial negotiation strategy, which remain with procurement, and out of scope is the operational risk framework itself and the enterprise risk register, into which third-party risk feeds but which is not owned by this programme. Out of scope is the bank's own internal controls and the first-party vendor management practices of its suppliers, other than where the bank has a contractual right to obtain assurance about them. Out of scope is vendor code of conduct and ESG assessment, which sit with human resources and sustainability.
objectives: Define the third-party population for the bank, resolve the three conflicting registers into a single source of truth and set a proportionate inclusion rule for smaller vendors.

Build a risk-based tiering model using objective criteria such as criticality of service, data sensitivity, access level, substitutability, regulatory exposure and concentration, and apply it consistently.
Design the full third-party lifecycle with defined entry criteria, required due diligence per tier, contract requirements, onboarding controls and exit provisions.

Produce a contract clause set proportionate to tier, including security, audit rights, incident notification timeframes, subcontractor approval, data location, exit assistance and termination for persistent failure.
Design an ongoing monitoring approach combining periodic reassessment, continuous signal monitoring and event-driven triggers, with clear thresholds.
Establish the treatment of a failed assessment, defining what happens at the vendor, the business owner and the board when a critical finding is not remediated.
Address concentration risk, particularly around the hyperscaler and the payment aggregator, and identify the substitution and exit options for tier-one vendors.
Map the programme onto the regulatory obligations and produce a board-approved third-party risk management policy with an implementation plan.
startingInformation: Procurement's vendor master has 612 active vendors; operational risk's register has 214; information security's assessment tracker has 96. The three lists have been reconciled by the GRC analyst and 41 vendors appear in only one list.

No tiering model exists. The bank's largest vendor by spend and its smallest by spend are both managed through the same annual questionnaire, and the questionnaire is returned by 71 percent of vendors with an average completion time of three days.

The payments aggregator failed an information security assessment twelve weeks ago with one critical finding on segregation of merchant onboarding data. The business unit accepted the risk verbally; there is no signed risk acceptance on file.

The KYC screening vendor moved customer identity data to a sub-processor in another country with no advance notice. No breach of the bank's own data was confirmed, but the bank's records of processing locations were wrong for four months.

No contract in the bank's portfolio for tier-one technology vendors contains a right to audit the vendor's premises or to obtain an independent assurance report. The standard template has a security annex with no audit clause.

A business process outsourcer handles 900 employees' worth of customer service and collections data from one site and has had two data incidents in the last eighteen months, both reported by the vendor within the contractual window.

The hyperscaler hosts three of the bank's cloud accounts and is also the primary provider for the payments platform and the customer analytics data warehouse; no exit plan exists and internal estimate of migration is 14 to 18 months.
The regulator's directions require board approval of a third-party risk management policy, a comprehensive third-party register, and oversight of outsourced activities as if internally performed.
The bank's enterprise risk register has 11 third-party risks; two are above appetite and both are owned by business heads who regard the vendor as a partner rather than a risk source.

Available budget is 1.2 crore rupees per year, which is primarily headcount for one third-party risk manager plus assessment tooling; the board has stated that the programme must not require new business budget from the retail or corporate business.
The outsourced assessment capability is limited: the bank can fund roughly 40 technical vendor assessments per year through its current supplier and has recently received quotes that would allow 70.

The bank's information security team believes the cloud provider's assurance reports (SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001) should be sufficient to discharge all monitoring obligations for tier-one vendors, which the risk team believes is unsafe.
activities: Extract the regulatory and supervisory expectations on third-party risk and translate them into a requirements register mapped to programme components.
Reconcile the three vendor registers into a single population, document the reconciliation logic, and set and apply an inclusion rule for low-materiality vendors.
Design and validate the tiering model with the business, information security, operational risk and procurement, including the criteria, the weights and the override mechanism for criticality.
Apply the tiering model to the population and analyse the resulting distribution, testing whether the outcome is credible for each tier-one and tier-two vendor.
Design the due diligence standard for each tier, specifying evidence required, who performs the assessment, independence requirements and what happens when evidence is inadequate.

Draft and negotiate the tiered contract clause set covering security, audit rights, incident notification, subcontractor and sub-processor approval, data location, service levels, exit assistance and termination.
Design the ongoing monitoring model: periodic reassessment intervals, continuous external signal monitoring, event-driven triggers and the escalation logic for each signal type.

Write the escalation and treatment protocol for failed assessments, including the acceptance authority matrix by severity and tier and the conditions under which a business relationship may continue despite an open critical finding.
Run a concentration analysis across tier-one vendors by service and by underlying infrastructure, and produce exit or substitution options with indicative lead times and costs.
Define the offboarding and exit management process including data return, deletion certification, credential revocation and continuity of service during exit.
Produce the board-approved third-party risk management policy and the operating procedures beneath it.
Build the implementation plan with phases, the required headcount and tooling, the reporting to the risk committee and the first-year milestones.
Present the programme and the remediation of the two specific live cases, the payments aggregator critical finding and the KYC sub-processor change, to the risk committee.
deliverables: Single reconciled third-party register with inclusion rules, tier assignments and data quality ratings
Third-party tiering model with criteria, weights, override rules and validation evidence
Tiered due diligence standard and ongoing monitoring framework with thresholds and escalation triggers
Tiered contract clause library with security, audit, incident notification, sub-processor, data location and exit provisions
Escalation and treatment protocol for failed vendor assessments with a severity-based acceptance authority matrix
Concentration risk analysis for tier-one vendors with exit and substitution options, lead times and indicative costs
Third-party offboarding and exit management procedure including data deletion certification and credential revocation
Board-approved third-party risk management policy and supporting operating procedures
Implementation roadmap with resourcing, tooling, reporting lines and first-year milestones
evaluationCriteria: The vendor population is reconciled and defensible. The inclusion rule for low-materiality vendors is explicit and the treatment of the 41 vendors found in one list only is addressed rather than tidied away.
The tiering model uses objective criteria with stated weights, has a validation step, and includes an override for criticality with governance over who may override it.
The applied tiering produces a credible distribution and the analyst has sanity-checked the outcomes against their knowledge of the business rather than accepting the model's output.
Due diligence and monitoring requirements are proportionate to tier and specify evidence, independence, frequency and escalation, rather than applying a questionnaire to everyone.

The contract clause library is realistic and specific, and the analyst addresses the harder question of how to obtain an audit right from a large hyperscaler, including what to do if it cannot be obtained.

The treatment of failed assessments is decisive. The payments aggregator case is worked through to a specific decision with the right acceptance authority, and the analyst does not let a verbal acceptance stand as the programme's model behaviour.
Concentration risk is analysed at the level of underlying infrastructure, not only at the level of named vendors, and the exit options carry realistic lead times and costs.
Offboarding is treated as a control with evidence, including data deletion certification, rather than as an administrative step.
The programme is mapped explicitly to the regulatory expectations, and the mapping shows where the bank currently falls short rather than asserting compliance.
The implementation plan is deliverable with the stated budget and does not quietly require new business funding that the board has ruled out.
items.modelSolution:
The instinct with a third-party programme is to start with the policy. Resist it. A third-party risk management programme that fails will fail because the vendor population is unknown, because tiering is subjective, and because nobody decides what happens when an assessment fails. Those three things have to be fixed before any policy is worth writing, because the policy's credibility is entirely borrowed from whether the underlying machinery works.

The first job is the population. Three registers with 612, 214 and 96 entries is not three views of a vendor base, it is three different ideas of what a vendor is. Reconcile them on a defined unit (the legal entity that signs the contract, not the brand), publish the reconciliation, and be honest about the 41 vendors that appear in one list only. Many will be micro-vendors, but some will be significant and unmanaged, and the programme's first finding should be those. Then set an explicit inclusion rule for low-materiality vendors, with a defined threshold, a light-touch annual attestation and a named owner. Excluding vendors from scope entirely is what makes programmes hollow; excluding them from full due diligence with a documented light regime is defensible.

Tiering is the mechanism that makes the rest affordable, and it is where programmes most often fail through vagueness. Build it from objective criteria rather than from spend: criticality of the service to a critical business process, sensitivity and volume of data accessed, extent of privileged access to the bank's environment or network, substitutability of the service, regulatory and conduct exposure, and concentration. Weight them, apply them, and then do the thing most analysts skip: sanity-check the output with the people who know the business. If a vendor that supports the payments hub has been tiered as medium, the model is wrong or the criteria are wrong, and you need to know which. Include an override for criticality and, importantly, specify who may override, because an uncontrolled override mechanism destroys the model's value.

The payments aggregator case should be used as the programme's design test rather than parked as a separate incident. It is a critical finding, it has been open for twelve weeks, and the business owner accepted it verbally. That is precisely the failure mode the programme exists to prevent. Work out the right design: a severity-based acceptance authority matrix, a time-limited acceptance with a mandatory remediation date, a requirement that acceptance is signed by someone with the authority to accept the business consequence rather than merely acknowledge the technical finding, and a defined condition under which the bank must suspend or exit. Then apply that design to the actual case and produce the specific decision the bank should be taking now, with the date by which it must be taken. A programme that cannot answer a live case will be judged on the live case.

The sub-processor incident points to a second structural gap: contract terms. Almost certainly no tier-one contract obliges the vendor to notify the bank before appointing a sub-processor, or to specify where data may be processed. That is a clause library problem, not an incident problem. Draft the clauses in tiers, including security requirements, audit rights, incident notification with a defined clock, sub-processor and sub-outsourcing approval with objection rights, data residency and transfer restrictions, business continuity and DR obligations, service levels with meaningful penalties, exit assistance and data return, and termination for persistent control failure. Then be honest about the hardest one, which is audit rights against a hyperscaler: you will not get premises audit rights from a major cloud provider, and pretending otherwise is dishonest. The realistic alternatives are independent assurance reports under agreed scope, a right to audit a sample of controls or to require a scoped assessment by the bank's assessor, contractual notification and cooperation obligations, and leveraging the bank's own security monitoring where it has it. Say that plainly in the programme and present the residual limitation to the committee.

On monitoring, resist the default of the annual questionnaire. A useful design has three inputs: periodic reassessment at a tier-based interval, continuous external signal monitoring for adverse news, breaches, regulatory action and certification lapses, and event-driven triggers, for example the vendor announcing a breach, a change of ownership, a new sub-processor, a regulatory investigation or a change of critical service. The monitoring standard should specify who acts on each signal and within what time. The questionnaire then becomes a confirmation step rather than the control itself.

Concentration risk deserves analysis at the level of underlying infrastructure, because the bank has three cloud accounts with one provider and the payments platform and analytics warehouse both sit on it. Two vendors in the register can fail simultaneously because they share infrastructure. That is a concentration finding that no vendor-by-vendor assessment will surface, and it is exactly the kind of insight the board has never been given. Produce it, with realistic exit lead times and indicative migration cost, and be honest that the answer for the payments platform may be a decision to accept concentration with documented compensating controls rather than an expensive migration that the bank cannot fund.

Offboarding is routinely the weakest control in this lifecycle and it has real evidentiary value. Specify credential revocation with independent verification, data return and deletion with certification, the removal of connectivity paths, the closure of monitoring, and continuity of service during exit. Treat it as a control that leaves evidence.

Finally, the regulatory mapping. Set out each supervisory expectation against what the bank does today and against what the programme will do, and mark the gaps honestly. The current state, with three disconnected registers, no tiering and no audit rights in any contract, is materially short of what is expected, and the board should hear that from you rather than discover it in an examination. The implementation plan has to fit 1.2 crore rupees, which realistically means one dedicated third-party risk manager, a defined assessment budget, and a phased first year that covers tier-one and tier-two vendors before extending. If the plan requires business units to fund assessments, say so and flag the consequence, because that is where programmes like this quietly die.
items.managementFeedback:
This is the first third-party proposal I have seen from inside this bank that treats the vendor register as a risk population rather than a procurement list. The reconciliation across the three registers was worth doing on its own; you identified eleven vendors that no function was actually managing, and two of them touch customer data, which nobody knew.

The tiering model is the part I need to defend to the board, so it needs to be stronger. The overrides are currently too easy: you have set criteria and weights but you have not specified who may override, and you know as well as I do that the payments aggregator's business head will come to you within a week asking for an override. If overrides are easy, tiering stops meaning anything and the programme becomes a queue of exceptions. Put a governance wrapper around the override and make the criteria explicit about substitutability, which is the one nobody has argued about properly and which is where the real concentration risk sits.

The payments aggregator case: I agree with your conclusion on the design, but I have not accepted the outcome yet. I am not signing a verbal acceptance, and I am not suspending a payments relationship that carries live merchant volume without a compensating assessment of customer impact. Your protocol needs to say what happens in that specific situation, not only in the abstract. That is the kind of detail that will decide whether the programme is real.

Two further points. The audit right against the hyperscaler is a genuinely useful piece of honesty and please keep it in the committee pack, because I would rather state the limitation than be found out on it. And the concentration analysis is the finding I expect to be asked about twice; the exit cost estimate needs a range with stated assumptions, because a single number will be treated as a commitment.

What would earn you a bigger role: I have watched three GRC people try to build a vendor programme here and none got past the register. You have a working model with a live case, a contract library and a costed plan. Put those in front of the risk committee yourself, with me in the room, and I will argue for you.

items.title: Create a business continuity and disaster recovery programme
items.background: Surya Telecom Ltd. is a fictional operator with 28 million mobile subscribers and 6,200 employees, operating 4G and 5G networks across 22 circles with 900 cell sites, 14 regional data centres and a central network operations centre, plus a consumer broadband business with 1.1 million customers and an enterprise connectivity segment serving 24,000 business customers. Its systems include the network element management layer, an operations support system and business support system, a customer self-care and e-commerce platform with 14 million registered users, an in-house payments wallet, and a spectrum and network planning stack. The telecom sector in India is governed by licence conditions that require operators to maintain high levels of network availability and to report service outages, and the company is also subject to the personal data protection obligations and the CERT-In reporting directions that apply to all organisations. Five months ago a power conditioning failure at the Chennai regional data centre took down the wallet platform and the e-commerce platform for 19 hours, during which 1.8 million recharge attempts failed; the recovery was completed by rebuilding environment configuration by hand because the runbooks were written for a version of the platform that had been retired two years earlier. A month later a nationwide DDoS campaign against the customer-facing portal succeeded in degrading the self-care application for four hours, and the incident response team discovered only because a customer tweeted it, not because a detection rule fired. The CTO inherited a BCP portfolio of 180 documents in a shared drive that has been untouched since 2022, a single recovery test in 2021, and a business impact analysis last refreshed in 2019 with pre-pandemic assumptions about call centre staffing. The board has mandated a genuine programme and has tied the CTO's annual incentive to reducing the time to restore tier-one services, while the operations director has warned that a realistic plan will expose business units whose continuity arrangements were never funded.
items.scope: In scope: all business services delivered by the company, covering mobile voice and data, fixed broadband, enterprise connectivity, the digital channels including the self-care portal and the wallet, retail and enterprise sales, customer service and field operations, network operations and the supporting IT platforms, and the shared corporate functions. In scope is the full continuity lifecycle: governance and policy, business impact analysis, the mapping of business services to the supporting technology, the critical business and technical services, recovery time and recovery point objectives, the continuity and disaster recovery strategies, plans, testing and exercise regime, crisis management, and the link to the enterprise risk register. Out of scope is the technical network resilience design owned by the radio and transmission engineering teams, beyond the interface with it. Out of scope is regulatory capital and liquidity continuity, which is not applicable to the company, and out of scope is the operational continuity plans of retail franchise and enterprise connectivity resellers, beyond a contractual and monitoring interface. Also out of scope is workforce planning in detail, which belongs to human resources, beyond the role in business impact analysis.
objectives: Define the continuity governance, including the accountable executive, the plan owners, the escalation and activation authority, and how the programme reports to the board.
Conduct a business impact analysis across business services and support functions, with realistic disruption scenarios and time-phased impact, replacing the 2019 assumptions.
Establish recovery time and recovery point objectives for each critical business and critical technical service, and secure agreement with the business on the cost of achieving them.

Map business services to supporting technology, third parties, people and premises, and identify the dependencies and single points of failure that the enterprise risk register does not currently capture.

Design a continuity strategy and a disaster recovery strategy that reflect the actual estate, including the cloud footprint, the data centre footprint and the manual workarounds the business relies on.
Produce prioritised, owned and resourced continuity plans for each business unit, replacing the 180 unreviewed documents with a manageable set.
Build a testing and exercise regime including a callaway test, a technical failover test, a scenario-based crisis exercise and an end-to-end test of the highest-criticality service.
Rehearse the Chennai data centre scenario specifically, since that is the highest-severity single-site failure mode, and determine whether the current configuration can be restored at all.
Deliver a costed improvement roadmap with board-level trade-offs between resilience investment and the revenue and churn consequences of outages.
startingInformation: Surya Telecom has 28 million mobile subscribers, 1.1 million broadband customers, 24,000 enterprise customers, 6,200 employees, 900 cell sites, 14 regional data centres and one central NOC.

The Chennai data centre outage five months ago caused 19 hours of wallet and e-commerce downtime and 1.8 million failed recharge attempts. Recovery took 11 hours beyond the initial outage because runbooks were outdated against the current platform version.
The nationwide DDoS four months ago degraded the self-care portal for four hours and was detected by a customer post rather than by a detection rule.
The BCP portfolio contains 180 documents in a shared drive, last edited in 2022. A single recovery test was performed in 2021 and its report has not been located.
The business impact analysis was last refreshed in 2019 and assumes call centre staffing of 1,100; the current establishment is 640 with an additional 380 outsourced.
Two cloud providers host the digital channels and enterprise platforms; a third cloud region is under consideration to address the concentration risk in the current two.
Fourteen regional data centres exist, of which six are in Tier 3 cities, and the company owns all of them; the customer-facing platforms run in two of the fourteen plus the two cloud providers.

Network planning shows that a total outage of a single regional data centre affects 1.1 million to 3.4 million subscribers depending on the circle, with the largest concentration in the Chennai and Pune regions.

The licence conditions require reporting of significant outages to the regulator, and there is an internal target of 99.5 percent service availability against a contractual 99.0 percent floor with service credits to enterprise customers.

The company has an insurance programme covering property and cyber but with a 30-day business interruption waiting period, and the last claim on the cyber policy was rejected because of an incident-notification condition.
The CFO has approved 3.5 crore rupees for the current financial year for resilience investment, with a request for a further 5 crore at mid-year if the roadmap justifies it.
The board has tied 20 percent of the CTO's annual incentive to reducing aggregate tier-one recovery time and 10 percent to a successful annual end-to-end test.

Human resources has confirmed that the current workforce planning model does not permit cross-training for single-operator roles in the NOC, the payments platform and the enterprise order management system.
activities: Review the licence conditions, the enterprise contracts, the insurance terms and the CERT-In obligations to build the compliance obligations register that the programme must satisfy.
Interview the business unit heads and the technology service owners to understand the services each business actually depends on and what a disruption means operationally and commercially.

Run the business impact analysis workshops using time-phased impact, including reputational, regulatory, contractual, safety and financial dimensions, with the outsourcing arrangements explicitly modelled.
Agree recovery time and recovery point objectives per critical business and critical technical service and, critically, obtain the business commitment to them.

Map business services to applications, infrastructure, third parties, people and premises, and identify the concentration points and single points of failure, including the shared platform ownership between the wallet and the e-commerce platform.
Review the incident history of the last two years to test the current assumptions about which scenarios are realistic and which are theoretical.

Design the disaster recovery architecture options for the highest-criticality platforms, comparing active-active, active-passive, warm standby and manual fallback, and quantify each in cost, time to recover and operational complexity.

Assess the third-party dependencies in the continuity model, particularly the cloud providers and the field logistics and outsourcer, and confirm their contractual continuity obligations and tested DR commitments.
Write and rationalise the continuity and disaster recovery plans, replacing the 180-document portfolio with a small set of owned, current and usable plans.
Build the crisis management structure, the crisis communication plan including regulator, customer and media notification triggers, and the decision rights for invoking it.
Design the testing and exercise programme with a graduated schedule from callaway through technical failover to a full end-to-end test, and run the callaway test and one scenario exercise.
Rehearse the Chennai data centre scenario, including the possibility that configuration must be rebuilt, and document the real recovery time and the gaps.
Build the costed resilience roadmap with board-level options, including accepting a lower tier of service in exchange for cost, and present it with the outage cost evidence.
Integrate the programme findings into the enterprise risk register and the group's audit plan, and agree the ongoing reporting and review cadence.
deliverables: BCP and DR policy with governance, roles, escalation and activation authority, approved at board level
Completed business impact analysis with time-phased impact, and the list of critical business and technical services
Agreed recovery time and recovery point objectives with documented business sign-off and the cost of achieving them
Service-to-technology, third party, people and premises dependency map with concentration and single points of failure identified
Disaster recovery strategy options paper with cost, recovery time and complexity comparison for tier-one platforms
Consolidated set of owned continuity and disaster recovery plans for each business unit and technology service
Crisis management and communication plan with regulator and customer notification triggers
Testing and exercise programme with schedule and completed callaway test and scenario exercise reports
Chennai data centre recovery rehearsal report with the actual achievable recovery time and identified gaps
Costed three-year resilience roadmap with options, board trade-offs and governance reporting plan
evaluationCriteria: The business impact analysis is realistic and time-phased, reflecting the actual 640-person establishment and the 380 outsourced staff rather than copying the 2019 figures.
Recovery objectives are agreed with the business, not imposed by IT, and the analysis shows the cost of achieving them rather than assuming they are free.
The dependency mapping identifies the genuine concentration points, including the shared platform ownership between the wallet and e-commerce platforms and the cloud provider concentration.

Recovery strategy options are compared on cost and recovery time with real assumptions, and manual or degraded-service modes are treated as legitimate choices with explicit decision triggers rather than as failure.
The outage history is used to challenge assumptions, and the Chennai scenario is rehearsed rather than asserted, with the true recovery time stated including the configuration rebuild risk.
The consolidated plan set is materially smaller and more usable than the 180-document portfolio it replaces, and each plan has a named owner and a review date.
Crisis management covers decision rights and the regulatory notification triggers, including the threshold for notifying the regulator and how it interacts with customer service credits.
The testing regime is graduated and real, and the analyst distinguishes a paper exercise from a genuine technical failover.
The roadmap presents genuine board options, including accepting reduced service levels, rather than a single non-negotiable capital request.
The work connects to the enterprise risk register and the audit plan rather than operating as an isolated project with no organisational home.
items.modelSolution:
The temptation in a BCP programme is to produce beautiful plans and beautiful diagrams and change nothing. The discipline that makes this programme work is to start from the two real incidents in the last five months, because they tell you what actually fails, and to use the business impact analysis to test the plan rather than the other way round.

Start with the Chennai outage. Nineteen hours of downtime, 1.8 million failed recharge attempts, and then eleven hours of additional recovery because the runbooks described a retired platform version. That single fact tells you the company's continuity capability for the wallet is effectively zero, because the plans did not correspond to the systems. Whatever else the programme does, it must begin by making the highest-criticality platforms actually recoverable. The right exercise is not another tabletop, it is a rehearsal: take the Chennai scenario, work out whether the configuration can be rebuilt from source at all or whether it exists only on the failed systems, and time it. If the honest answer is that a rebuild takes four days rather than four hours, the board needs to know that before it sets expectations with enterprise customers.

The DDoS is the second anchor. Four hours of degradation detected by a customer post tells you the detection regime is not monitoring for the thing that matters. Include that in the programme as a monitoring and detection objective with a specific detection time target, because resilience without detection is just availability for the attacks that were lucky.

Now the business impact analysis. Do not copy the 2019 document. Re-interview every business unit head, because the shape of the business has changed: the digital channels are now a much larger share of revenue, the enterprise segment has service credits attached, and there is a wallet that has become material to revenue in a way it was not in 2019. Model impact in phases, because a two-hour outage and a two-day outage are different events for the enterprise segment even if the number of affected customers is the same. Include the outsourcing arrangement explicitly in the staffing picture, since 380 of the 1,020 contact-centre positions are now outsourced and their continuity is a contractual question the company does not control.

Then the step that most BCP programmes skip and that this one must not: agree the recovery objectives with the business and price them. The board of a telecom company will not accept a target of four-hour recovery for every service, because that is enormously expensive and pointless for a back-office process. Get the business to say which hours matter and which do not, then compute what each objective costs in technology, in run cost and in test frequency. The output is not a uniform target; it is a small number of services with genuinely aggressive objectives, a larger number with reasonable ones, and an explicit list of services that will run in degraded mode with a stated trigger for invocation. Degraded mode is a legitimate strategy and treating it as one, with a decision rule, is what makes the plan affordable.

Do the dependency mapping carefully, because that is where the real concentration risk shows up. The wallet and the e-commerce platform share ownership of a platform, which means one team and one deployment pipeline is a single point of failure for two revenue streams. Two cloud providers hold the digital channels, and the Pune region concentration affects up to 3.4 million subscribers. The insurance programme has a 30-day business interruption waiting period and the last cyber claim was rejected on a notification condition, which means insurance is not a recovery strategy for anything on the near-term horizon. Each of these should appear as a finding with a route into the enterprise risk register, and at least two should end up as named risks with an executive owner.

For the disaster recovery architecture, compare options honestly for the tier-one platforms. Active-active for the wallet is expensive but the wallet drives prepaid revenue and the outage history makes it painful. Active-passive for the e-commerce platform may be proportionate. Warm standby plus a manual fallback for enterprise order management might be right, because the manual process exists and works, and a fully automated DR solution for a process with 40 daily orders would be a bad investment. A manual fallback with a clear trigger, tested, is a legitimate control. Make the trade-off explicit and let the board see the cost of each option against the outage cost, which you can now estimate from the recharge failure data and the enterprise service credit exposure.

Consolidate the plan portfolio ruthlessly. 180 unreviewed documents in a shared drive are worse than nothing, because they create false confidence. The output should be a small set of owned plans: one per business unit, one per technology service tier, one crisis management plan and one set of communication templates. Each with an owner who can actually be contacted at 3am, a review date and a last-tested date. Then make the plan real by walking through the Chennai scenario with the people who would execute it and capturing every step where the plan says something that is not true.

The crisis management piece must be specific about regulatory notification. The company has licence conditions and outage reporting obligations, and there are enterprise contracts with credits that trigger on an availability breach. Define the thresholds and the decision owner for each, and be careful about the interaction between notifying the regulator and the commercial consequences of that notification, because the board will want to know how those trade off.

Finally, the roadmap and the governance. The 3.5 crore already approved should buy the rehearsed recovery of the tier-one platforms, the detection improvement and the exercise regime. The additional 5 crore should be requested only for the specific options where the board has been shown the outage cost and the capital cost side by side. And the reporting cadence should be quarterly to the board risk committee with a single page per critical service showing last test date, last actual recovery time and the gap to target, because a programme that reports only during exercises is a programme that decays quietly.
items.managementFeedback:
The most valuable thing in this work is that you started with our own incidents rather than with a template. Most consultants would have handed me a BCP document with a matrix of criticality ratings and no mention of the fact that our runbooks described a platform we retired two years ago. Yours begins with that, and it changes the credibility of everything that follows.

Two things I want to push on. First, the recovery time objectives. You have asked the business for sign-off and I suspect you have not got it for the enterprise segment, because the enterprise business heads want four-hour recovery and the technology team cannot deliver it inside the current budget. Do not let this become a negotiation you lose by default. Show me the option set with costs and let me take the trade-off to the business myself. What I will not accept is a plan that quietly promises something the technology cannot deliver, because the first time that is tested with a customer watching, this stops being a GRC problem and becomes a commercial dispute.

Second, the manual fallback for enterprise order management. I like the argument, but I have watched manual processes fail under pressure in a way IT processes do not. If you are going to recommend degraded mode as a strategy, the manual process needs to be exercised and timed with the same rigour as a technical failover, and it needs an owner who accepts that it might be used on a Sunday night when the volume is low. I want that owner named in the plan rather than inferred.

The testing programme is well designed, but the graduated approach has an obvious failure mode, which is that the first exercise is always a paper exercise and everyone enjoys it, and then the technical failover slips to the following year because the Christmas freeze period starts. Push the technical failover into the freeze window deliberately, or it will never happen.

What would make me back you for a larger role: you have produced the first continuity analysis in this company that a customer-facing business head actually read without asking you to explain it. The next step is proving it, and the thing that would help me most is a rehearsal of Chennai that produces a real time and a real list of gaps, even though the answer will be ugly.

items.title: Perform a SOC 2 readiness assessment
items.background: Kiteframe Software Pvt. Ltd. is a fictional B2B software company of 320 employees founded in Bengaluru, selling a cloud workflow and analytics platform used by 780 industrial and logistics customers under a multi-tenant architecture on a single public cloud provider, with 41 million events ingested per day. Revenue is 84 percent subscription and the company has grown 2.4 times in two years, which means the security function has been outpaced: there are four people in security and engineering, the SOC is outsourced to a provider that only receives alerts in a shared channel, and the engineering team of 60 grew from 22. A large enterprise customer whose contract renews in five months requires a SOC 2 Type II report covering the security and availability trust services criteria as a condition of renewal, and their procurement team has already asked for the auditor's name and the observation period, which the company does not have. The chief executive has begun referring to the company as SOC 2 certified in customer conversations, which creates a live expectation the company cannot currently meet. A penetration test eleven months ago found a critical privilege escalation path from a developer role to the production database and a high-severity issue with how tenant data isolation was enforced in one export path, both of which were fixed without a formal change record. The company uses eleven sub-processors for email, messaging, monitoring, support and error tracking, one of which is a support platform in another country that was added without a data processing agreement and is not listed on the company's website. A finance team member with elevated reporting access in the billing system has been in post for three years and the review of that access is overdue. A trusted adviser has told the chief executive that the realistic path is to complete a readiness assessment now, remediate the gaps in a focused eight-week window, then evidence the three to six month observation period and use the first annual report as the vehicle for the renewal.
items.scope: In scope: the security and availability trust services criteria applied to the Kiteframe product platform and the corporate environment that supports it, including the multi-tenant application, the cloud infrastructure, identity and access management, change management and the software development lifecycle, production access and privileged operations, logging and monitoring, incident response, vendor and sub-processor management, physical and environmental controls including the outsourced hosting, and the people and governance controls that relate to security. The assessment covers the observation period the company should plan for, the controls that must operate for the whole of it, and the evidence that will be produced for each. Out of scope is the confidentiality and privacy criteria, which are a separate engagement and are not required by the customer, and out of scope is the financial statement criteria. Out of scope is the detailed technical verification of the platform's product security beyond what the criteria require, including the earlier penetration test findings, which are handled by the engineering remediation track. Out of scope is the customer's own controls and any assessment of the sub-processors' internal controls beyond obtaining their assurance reports.
objectives: Establish the engagement perimeter, the trust services criteria to be covered, the audit period that will be required and the boundaries of the system, and confirm this with the customer and the prospective auditor.
Produce the control matrix mapping each in-scope criterion to a control, a frequency, an owner and the specific artefact that will serve as evidence.
Perform a gap assessment against the criteria by testing the current environment rather than by reading policies, and classify each gap as a design gap, an operating gap or an evidence gap.

Address the specific issues already known: the penetration test remediation without change records, the missing sub-processor data processing agreement, the unlisted sub-processor, the overdue access review and the absence of an incident response plan.
Design the eight-week remediation plan with owners, sequencing, dependencies and the specific evidence each remediation will produce.
Define the observation period strategy, including which controls must operate from day one of the period and how evidence will be captured automatically rather than assembled manually.
Assess the feasibility and timeline of the customer renewal, and prepare an honest options analysis for the chief executive covering accelerate, extend or restructure.
Produce the readiness report and the executive summary that the chief executive can use to correct the SOC 2 certified expectation in customer conversations.
startingInformation: Kiteframe has 320 employees, 780 customer tenants on a multi-tenant platform, and 41 million events ingested per day with a 99.9 percent uptime target committed in customer contracts.
There is no information security policy set beyond a one-page acceptable use document; the general privacy policy is a customer-facing web page last updated 14 months ago.

Four people work in security and engineering (one security engineer, one cloud engineer, one detection engineer, one GRC analyst, which is the role you are filling), and engineering is 60 people including 22 who can deploy to production.
The security team is entirely within engineering, with no independent reporting line, and the SOC is outsourced to a provider that receives alerts only in a shared Slack channel.

A penetration test eleven months ago returned one critical privilege escalation finding from a developer role to the production database and one high-severity tenant data isolation issue in an export path; both were fixed in the same sprint with no change record and no evidence that a retest was performed.

The company uses eleven sub-processors. One, a customer support platform hosted outside India, was added eight months ago with no data processing agreement, and it is not listed on the website sub-processor page that three enterprise customers have asked to see.
Access reviews have been performed ad hoc. The last full review was 14 months ago; a finance team member with elevated reporting access in the billing system has been in post for three years.

There is no formal incident response plan. Two incidents in the last year, a customer data export error affecting 6 tenants and an availability event, were handled informally by the engineering on-call rotation.

The cloud environment is a single provider with one production account and two non-production accounts. Production database access for engineers is granted through a bastion host with session recording that is enabled but whose recordings are retained for 30 days and are not reviewed.
The customer requiring SOC 2 has a renewal date in five months and a procurement team that has asked for the auditor's name, the audit criteria and the observation period start date.

Cost estimates received: the audit firm has quoted 9 to 13 lakh rupees depending on observation period length, with an additional 4 lakh for a readiness gap assessment; the current security tooling spend is 5 lakh per year.
The chief executive has told two prospects in the last month that the company is SOC 2 certified and has committed in one sales proposal to delivering a Type II report within 90 days.
activities: Hold a scoping session with the customer procurement and security teams to confirm the criteria in scope, the reporting period, the auditor's requirements and what the customer will do with the report.
Engage an audit firm and agree the readiness gap assessment scope, the criteria coverage and the plan for the observation period, including what the auditor will sample and how often.
Define the system boundary and the in-scope infrastructure, applications, people and locations, and document the exclusions with justifications.
Build the criteria to control matrix with frequency, owner and named evidence artefact for every control, which becomes the operating manual for the observation period.

Test the current environment against the matrix with technique, including identity and access provisioning, privileged access, change management sampling, logging and alerting coverage, and vendor management.
Re-perform the 2024 penetration test findings, confirming that the fixes are in place and that the change records and retest evidence now exist.
Design and implement the incident response plan with severity definitions, roles, notification commitments and a test record, and run one internal tabletop.

Remediate the sub-processor position: execute the missing data processing agreement, publish the accurate sub-processor list, and confirm the support platform's security posture with its assurance report.
Perform a full production and privileged access review, remediate the exceptions including the long-standing elevated billing access, and put a recurring quarterly review in place with evidence.
Establish logging and monitoring coverage for the cloud environment, the application and the production database, with a documented detection use case set and a review cadence.

Build the continuous evidence collection mechanism so that change records, access reviews, backup restore tests, vulnerability scans and incident tickets are captured automatically during the observation period.

Prepare the options analysis for the chief executive comparing an accelerated timeline, a renewal-date negotiation and a restructured customer commitment, with the commercial and regulatory consequences of each.
Deliver the readiness report with the gap register, the remediation plan, the observation period plan and the residual risk statement, and present it to the executive team and the board.
deliverables: SOC 2 readiness assessment report with system boundary, criteria scope and audit period recommendation
Criteria to control matrix with frequency, owner and named evidence artefact for every in-scope control
Gap register classifying each gap as design, operating or evidence, with severity and remediation owner
Detailed evidence and observation period plan with the controls that must operate from day one of the period
Remediated and evidenced penetration test findings including change records and retest results
Incident response plan with severity definitions, escalation, notification commitments and a completed tabletop record
Sub-processor pack including the executed data processing agreement, the accurate published sub-processor list and the assurance evidence for each sub-processor
Completed privileged access review report and the standing quarterly access review procedure
Eight-week remediation plan with owners, dependencies and the evidence each action produces
Executive options analysis on the audit timeline against the customer renewal, with commercial consequences
evaluationCriteria: The criteria scope, system boundary and audit period recommendation are confirmed against an audit firm and the customer requirement rather than assumed, and the exclusions are justified in writing.
The control matrix is complete for the criteria in scope, with a frequency and a named evidence artefact for each control, and functions as the operating manual for the observation period.

The gap assessment distinguishes design gaps, operating gaps and evidence gaps. An evidence gap where the control works but produces no artefact is identified separately, because it is the most common cause of a failed report.
The assessment tests rather than surveys, and the sample-based conclusions are evidenced with artefacts and dates rather than attestations.

The known issues are dealt with directly, including the penetration test fixes lacking change records and retest, the missing sub-processor agreement, the unpublished sub-processor and the overdue access review.
The incident response plan is specific, includes notification commitments that match customer contracts, and has been exercised at least once with a written record.

The observation period plan is realistic about which controls must operate for the full period and builds evidence collection into the operating rhythm so that the final months are not an evidence-gathering exercise.
The options analysis is honest with the chief executive, correcting the SOC 2 certified expectation and presenting a renewal-date risk that a customer may not accept.
The remediation plan is sequenced by dependency, sized against the 9 to 13 lakh audit cost and the 5 lakh annual tooling spend, and assigns owners who can actually deliver.
The residual risk statement is clear about what will still not be demonstrated at report date, rather than implying full readiness.
items.modelSolution:
The commercial pressure in this scenario is real and it shapes everything, so begin by converting it into a clear timeline problem. The customer requires a Type II report. A Type II report covers a period during which controls operated, so the question is not when the audit starts but when the observation period can begin, and the honest answer is that the clock starts only once controls designed for the criteria are in place and operating. That gives a fixed arithmetic: an eight-week remediation window, then a three to six month observation period, then the report, and any customer date that does not sit beyond that is not achievable. The first job is to make that arithmetic visible to the chief executive, because the alternative is a company that discovers in month six that it has missed a renewal it has already promised.

Alongside that, correct the expectation. The company has told two prospects it is SOC 2 certified, which is a false claim in substance and a legal problem in practice, since the SOC 2 report is an attestation by an independent CPA firm and the company cannot self-certify. A professional firm will also refuse to issue a report that states or implies coverage the customer did not contract, so the marketing language has to change now rather than at report date.

Scope next, and do it with an auditor rather than alone. The customer named security and availability, which is narrower than the full set and materially cheaper, but the scope boundary still needs work: what is the system, what infrastructure is in, what is excluded and why. The cloud provider's own SOC 2 report and ISO certificate can be used for some infrastructure controls, but the company has to accept and manage that residual risk explicitly rather than assuming the inheritance is automatic. Bring the auditor in early, even if only for a scoping conversation, because the standard assumption that an audit is a two-week event at the end is exactly what produces a failed first report.

The control matrix is the backbone of the programme. For each criterion, one control, one frequency, one named owner and one specific artefact. The specificity of the artefact matters more than the elegance of the mapping, because a criterion like logical access requires an artefact that shows the review happened and what it found, not a policy that says reviews happen. Where the current process produces an artefact only with effort, redesign the process so the artefact is produced by doing the work rather than by remembering to document it afterwards. That is the difference between an observation period that runs cleanly and one that becomes three weeks of evidence archaeology in the final month.

Classify the gaps properly, because the three types need different responses. A design gap means the control does not exist and must be built, which is the eight-week work. An operating gap means the control exists and is sometimes not performed, which needs supervision and enforcement. An evidence gap means the control is performed and works but produces nothing an auditor can inspect, which needs only instrumentation and is the cheapest to fix. Most readiness assessments lump these together and then build a plan that is too expensive and too slow, because they treat an evidence gap as a design gap. The sub-processor list on the website is an evidence gap; the absence of an incident response plan is a design gap; the elevated billing access is an operating gap that has now compounded into a real access risk.

On the known issues, do not simply confirm they are fixed. The penetration test findings were closed in a sprint with no change record and no retest, which means the company has a false closure and no evidence. Re-perform the retest, reconstruct the change record honestly with a note explaining the gap, and note the process failure in the report. Similarly with the sub-processor: execute the agreement, publish the accurate list, and obtain the supplier's assurance report rather than assuming the support platform is fine because it has never had an incident. The overdue access review is the one most likely to produce an unwelcome finding, so do it properly with a documented population, evidence of review and remediation of the three-year-old elevated access, and then put a recurring quarterly review in place with a calendar entry and a named owner.

Two structural weaknesses need to be addressed because an auditor will test them. The SOC being an outsourced provider fed by a Slack channel is not a defensible monitoring control; it needs defined alert sources, a documented response workflow and a retained record of triage, even if the triage is performed by the outsourced team. And the bastion host's session recordings, retained for 30 days and never reviewed, are a strong control implemented badly; extend the retention to cover the audit period, add review of a sample of privileged sessions to a defined cadence, and make that review an evidenced control.

The incident response plan needs to be written for a company of this size, which means short, specific and exercised. Severity definitions tied to customer impact, named roles with a real escalation path, a customer notification commitment that matches the 72-hour clauses in customer contracts, a documented process for the two notification channels, and a record of an internal tabletop. One exercise produces evidence that the plan has been operated, which is worth a great deal.

Then the observation period plan, which is the piece most organisations neglect. Identify the controls that must operate for the full period, because those are the ones that need to be right on day one: access reviews, change management, vulnerability management, incident management, backup and restore testing, and privileged access monitoring. Build the evidence capture into the operating rhythm. If the company is going to hand an auditor three months of evidence assembled by hand in the final fortnight, the report will be late or thin, and the customer renewal will be missed.

Finally, the options analysis for the executive. Present three honestly: accelerate by funding the tooling and contractors to compress the remediation and shorten the observation period to the regulatory minimum, which is expensive and risky; hold the realistic timeline and open a commercial conversation with the customer now, which is usually better than a late report; or restructure the customer commitment to a mutually agreed security exhibit with a defined roadmap, which trades a certification for a negotiated alternative. Give each a cost, a risk and a consequence, and put the recommendation in front of the chief executive rather than making the choice implicitly. The residual risk statement should say plainly which criteria will not be fully demonstrated at report date, because that is the difference between a professional readiness assessment and a sales document.
items.managementFeedback:
This is the assessment I needed and, more importantly, it is the assessment I could have used to walk into the customer conversation with a plan rather than a hope. The timeline arithmetic in the executive options paper is the part I will take to the board, because it converts a fuzzy promise into a date and a cost.

Three pushbacks. First, the SOC 2 certified language. You have addressed it in the report and I have acted on it in the two sales conversations, which is the right outcome, but I want you to understand why it happened: we are a 320-person company selling to enterprise buyers, and certification is a procurement gate that our competitors pass and we did not. You will be judged on whether we pass it, so please do not soften the timeline in future documents to make my life easier. If the realistic answer is six months, write six months.

Second, the incident response plan. It is good, and the tabletop record is exactly what an auditor wants, but I want to see one more thing: a documented link between the severity you defined and the notification clauses in our top 20 customer contracts. If those do not line up, we have a contractual exposure that is not a GRC issue but a legal one, and I need to know this month.

Third, the remediation plan is realistic but the owner list worries me. Several owners are individuals in engineering who are already on the critical path for the 2.4 times growth we have had. If the plan depends on their goodwill, it will slip, and a slip here directly costs us the renewal. Where you have named an individual, tell me the manager who will make it happen.

What would make me back you for a bigger job: you told me in week two that the certification claim was a legal problem I did not know I had, before I asked. That is the behaviour I want to see repeatedly. Bring me bad news early and I will give you the room to fix it.

items.title: Develop a regulatory compliance register for an Indian financial organisation
items.background: Vanguard Financial Services Ltd. is a fictional 5,000-employee universal bank headquartered in Mumbai, providing retail and corporate banking through 640 branches, with a 180-person IT operations team, a 24x7 security operations centre, a Chennai data centre and a growing portfolio of cloud workloads. It is a scheduled commercial bank supervised by the Reserve Bank of India, holds a universal banking licence, and has two regulated subsidiaries: a capital markets subsidiary that runs a brokerage and a mutual fund distribution business, and a wholly owned insurance subsidiary that sells group life and general insurance. The bank is consequently subject to the supervisory expectations of three regulators, and its subsidiaries are separately supervised with their own reporting. A regulator inspection closed six months ago with seven observations, two of which concerned the absence of a consolidated view of regulatory obligations across the group and the absence of an owned, dated remediation plan for the observations, and both observations remain open. The bank has a compliance function of 38 people, an enterprise risk function of 54, an internal audit function of 38 and a legal function of 21, and the four have historically each maintained their own reading of the supervisory requirements, which means the bank's actual exposure to any single obligation is rarely known to anyone outside that function. The board risk committee receives a regulatory update once a quarter produced by the Chief Compliance Officer, and that update has historically been a narrative of recent supervisory letters rather than a register of obligations. A new Chief Compliance Officer joined four months ago and has been asked by the board to produce a regulatory compliance register that shows, for the bank and its subsidiaries, which obligations apply, who owns them, what evidence demonstrates compliance, when the last evidence was seen and what the residual exposure is. She has also warned that the first version of any such register will be wrong in several material respects and that finding those errors is the real work.
items.scope: In scope: all regulatory and supervisory obligations applying to Vanguard Financial Services Ltd. and its two regulated subsidiaries, covering prudential and conduct directions of the banking regulator, the listing and market conduct obligations applicable to the capital markets subsidiary, the insurance obligations applicable to the insurance subsidiary, the anti-money laundering and countering financing of terrorism framework as it applies to the bank, the data protection obligations arising from the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and its rules, the CERT-In incident reporting directions, foreign exchange and related obligations, and any obligation arising from the bank's own contracts and licences such as network and payment system approvals. In scope is the obligations identification and mapping, ownership, evidence identification and testing, the gap and remediation process, and the reporting model. Out of scope is legal advice on the interpretation of any obligation, which remains with legal, and out of scope is the tax compliance function, which sits in finance and is covered by the group's tax governance. Out of scope is the detailed content of the subsidiaries' own supervisory submissions, and out of scope is prudential capital adequacy, which is owned by the Chief Risk Officer.
objectives: Define the perimeter of the register, covering the bank and both subsidiaries, and agree the definition of an obligation that is tracked.
Extract and catalogue the regulatory obligations from the primary sources, recording citation, applicability, frequency and the date of the source version.
Map each obligation to the responsible function and a named accountable owner, and resolve the ownership gaps where no function currently owns an obligation.
Determine the evidence that demonstrates compliance for each obligation, including the periodicity of that evidence and where it is retained.
Test a representative sample of obligations to establish the true compliance state rather than the asserted state, and classify findings as gaps, partial compliance and evidences of non-compliance.
Link obligations to the enterprise risk register so that breaches of obligations become risks with a consequence, rather than staying as compliance observations.
Design the ongoing regulatory change management process, including how new circulars, directions and supervisory observations are triaged and assigned.
Design the reporting model to the board risk committee and to the regulator-facing governance forums, replacing narrative updates with exception-based reporting.
Produce a remediation plan for the seven open inspection observations and the identified gaps, with owners, dates and evidence of closure.
startingInformation: The group has 5,000 employees, 640 branches, a 180-person IT operations team, a 34-person SOC, a Chennai data centre and three cloud accounts.

Regulators in scope: the Reserve Bank of India as the primary supervisor of the bank, the securities regulator for the capital markets subsidiary which holds a stock exchange membership and a mutual fund distribution licence, and the insurance regulator for the insurance subsidiary which has an IRDAI registration.

The compliance function has 38 people, enterprise risk 54, internal audit 38 and legal 21; none of the four has a consolidated obligations register and each has its own partially maintained inventory.

The most recent supervisory inspection closed six months ago with seven observations, of which two remain open: the absence of a consolidated view of regulatory obligations across the group, and the absence of an owned and dated remediation plan for the observations themselves.

A supervisory letter issued eleven weeks ago asked the bank to explain its exposure to third-party and cloud concentration risk, and the response was prepared by operational risk without reference to the compliance register, because no such register exists.

The CERT-In directions require reporting specified incidents within six hours and require internet-facing systems to retain logs for 180 days; the bank's log retention on two legacy platforms is 30 days and no one in IT owns the compliance consequence of that.

The bank's data protection programme operates on a consent-based model with a privacy policy last updated 18 months ago, and the data protection officer has raised the absence of a Data Protection Board notification path for the subject rights process.

The bank's anti-money laundering programme has a full risk-based assessment, but a recent external audit found the sanctions screening coverage for the two subsidiaries is not integrated with the bank's own screening.
The Chief Compliance Officer has 2.4 crore rupees of budget, most of which is committed to the transaction monitoring system refresh, leaving under 40 lakh for programme and tooling.

The board risk committee meets quarterly and has never seen a single-page view of regulatory obligations; the last quarterly regulatory update was 14 pages and no decisions were recorded in the minutes.

Three new supervisory instruments have been issued in the last two quarters covering third-party risk, digital payment security and information security governance, and no one has read all three in full.
Internal audit has an audit of the regulatory compliance monitoring process scheduled for the next cycle and has asked whether a register exists that the audit could rely on.
activities: Agree the perimeter and the register's definition of an obligation with the Chief Compliance Officer, legal and the subsidiary compliance leads, and document what is deliberately out of scope.
Inventory the primary regulatory sources applicable to each entity in the perimeter, with version, date and the responsible reader, and prioritise by supervisory examination relevance.
Read and extract the obligations from the primary sources, capturing citation, obligation text in the regulator's own framing, applicability, frequency, and the date from which it applies.
Map obligations to internal policies, procedures, systems and controls, and identify the obligations with no internal counterpart, which are the highest-value findings.
Assign a named accountable owner to every obligation, resolving the ownership gaps by negotiation with the business and recording the escalation where ownership is refused.

Define the evidence standard for each obligation, including what artefact, how frequently refreshed, and where it is retained, and build a common taxonomy so that evidence types are comparable across obligations.
Test a representative sample of at least 20 obligations across the bank and both subsidiaries, using the evidence rather than management assertion, and record the true compliance state.
Classify the test results into compliant, partially compliant, non-compliant and not applicable, with the definition of each classification agreed and documented before testing begins.
Link every identified gap and every non-compliance to the enterprise risk register, with a risk consequence, an owner and a residual risk acceptance where applicable.
Design the regulatory change management process covering intake, triage, impact assessment, ownership assignment, implementation tracking and closure, with service levels.
Design the exception-based reporting model for the board risk committee, including the escalation thresholds that require a committee decision rather than a status update.
Prepare the remediation plan for the two open inspection observations and the gaps found in testing, with owners, dates and the evidence of closure that will satisfy the regulator.
Present the register design, the testing results and the remediation plan to the Chief Compliance Officer, the risk committee and, in a dry run, to the internal audit team.
deliverables: Regulatory compliance register specification with perimeter, obligation definition, classification scheme and ownership rules
Master obligations catalogue with citation, applicability, frequency, effective date and source version for each obligation
Obligation to internal control and evidence mapping with a standard evidence taxonomy
Ownership matrix with named accountable owners and a record of escalated ownership disputes
Regulatory test pack and results for the 20 obligations tested, with sampling method and evidence references
Gap classification and the linkage of every gap to an enterprise risk with consequence and owner
Regulatory change management process with intake, triage, impact assessment, assignment and closure service levels
Exception-based board reporting pack and the quarterly reporting calendar for the risk committee
Remediation plan for the two open inspection observations and the testing gaps, with owners, dates and closure evidence
Methodology note and resourcing plan for maintaining the register within the constrained budget
evaluationCriteria: The obligation definition, the classification scheme and the evidence standard are agreed and documented before testing starts, so that the findings are reproducible rather than a matter of opinion.
Obligations are extracted from primary sources with citation, applicability, frequency and effective date rather than summarised from secondary summaries or from memory.
Ownership is assigned to named accountable owners, and the ownership gaps that could not be resolved are escalated in writing rather than left blank.
The register distinguishes obligation, control and evidence, and the mapping shows where an obligation has no internal counterpart, which is the highest-value output.
Testing is performed against evidence for at least 20 obligations across all three regulated entities, and the sample and method are stated.
Findings are classified consistently with the pre-agreed definitions, and non-compliance is not softened into partial compliance for reasons of convenience.
Every gap and non-compliance is linked to the enterprise risk register with a consequence, so that regulatory exposure is visible in the enterprise risk view.
The change management process is operational, with named service levels and a stated treatment of an obligation that cannot be implemented in time.
The board reporting is exception-based with escalation thresholds, and would allow a committee member to identify what needs a decision in under two minutes.
The first version is presented as a starting position with known errors and a plan for correction, which reflects how the Chief Compliance Officer framed the task.
items.modelSolution:
