The framing from the Chief Compliance Officer, that the first version will be wrong in several material respects and that finding those errors is the real work, is exactly right, and the register has to be built to make errors findable. That is a design constraint that should drive the whole approach: a register that is clean on day one and wrong on day ninety is worse than one that is visibly provisional on day one and correct by day sixty.

Start with the definition of an obligation, and agree it before collecting anything. If an obligation means anything from a statutory provision to an internal policy statement, the register will become a document repository and will never be maintained. The workable definition is narrower: a requirement imposed by a regulator or a supervisory body in a binding instrument, that applies to the bank or to a subsidiary, and that creates an obligation on a recurring basis. One-off undertakings given in the course of an inspection may be tracked separately as commitments rather than obligations, which keeps the register clean and ensures they are not lost.

Perimeter next, and treat the group structure honestly. The bank, the capital markets subsidiary and the insurance subsidiary have different regulators, and the obligations that arise from the group's own operations often fall across entity boundaries in ways that are easy to miss. The bank's centralising choices, for example the shared sanctions screening and the group data protection programme, mean a single control serves three regulatory regimes, and the register must show that rather than triplicating the control and losing the insight. Make the perimeter explicit at the legal entity level, and note explicitly which subsidiary obligations the bank will meet centrally and on whose shoulders the accountability sits.

Collection should be primary-source and versioned. Read the actual circulars, directions and frameworks, and capture the citation, the date of the instrument, the date from which it applies and a note of what changed in each revision. This matters more than it sounds: the last three quarters alone have brought new supervisory instruments on third-party risk, digital payment security and information security governance, and no one in the bank has read all three. Build a source register first, with a named reader for each source, a read date and a triage decision, then extract obligations from the sources that survive triage. Prioritise by supervisory examination relevance rather than by document length, because a full read of every instrument is not achievable and pretending otherwise produces a shallow register.

The obligation to internal control mapping is where the real value appears. Take each obligation and ask the operational question: what do we actually do, where is it written down, what system enforces it, and what evidence would we show a supervisor. The obligations with no internal counterpart are the ones that matter, and there will be several that the bank has never consciously accepted. The log retention point is an example: the CERT-In direction requires 180 days of logs on internet-facing systems, two legacy platforms retain 30 days, and nobody in IT currently owns the compliance consequence. That is an obligation with a control that is operating to a different standard and no owner for the gap. Finding those and giving them an owner and a date is more valuable than a complete-looking register.

Ownership is the hardest and most valuable part of the work. Every obligation needs a named accountable owner in a business or control function, not in the compliance function, because the compliance function cannot discharge an obligation it does not own. Expect to encounter refusal, particularly where the owner believes the obligation is somebody else's, and expect to encounter a compliance function that quietly absorbs ownership to keep the register complete. Resist the second one explicitly, because a compliance function that owns 200 obligations owns none of them. Where ownership is genuinely contested, escalate it in writing with a proposed default and a date, and let the Chief Compliance Officer arbitrate. Where the owner refuses, record it as an explicit gap rather than hiding it.

Evidence is where the register becomes usable. Define a small common taxonomy of evidence types, for example policy with approval record, configuration export, system log extract, third-party assurance report, committee minute, training completion record, reconciliation output, and independent test report. Every obligation then maps to an evidence type and a refresh frequency. The benefit is comparability: when a supervisor asks for evidence on twenty obligations at once, the bank can produce it in a day rather than in a month of bespoke requests. That single property is what makes a register worth its maintenance cost, and it should be stated to the board as the primary benefit rather than as compliance with a requirement.

Testing is where the register's credibility is established. Test at least twenty obligations across all three entities, choosing a mix: some the bank believes are fully compliant, some where the bank suspects partial coverage, and some where the ownership is contested. Use evidence, not attestations. The point is not to find a high number of failures, it is to calibrate the register's claimed states against reality, and then to publish the calibration. Where the register says compliant and the evidence says otherwise, the register is wrong, and correcting it openly is what builds the compliance function's credibility with the business and with the regulator.

Classification must be pre-agreed and applied consistently. Compliant, partially compliant, non-compliant and not applicable, each with a written definition and an illustrative example, agreed with the Chief Compliance Officer before testing. Without that, the outcome becomes a negotiation, and partially compliant becomes a category that absorbs everything uncomfortable.

Then link every gap to the enterprise risk register. A regulatory non-compliance has a consequence, which is a risk, and it belongs in the risk view the board already sees. This linkage is also what stops the register becoming a compliance silo, and it is what will let the Chief Risk Officer use the register as an input rather than duplicating the work.

The change management process should be short and specific: intake from a named mailbox with the source index maintained, triage within a defined number of days with a named triage owner, impact assessment with a standard questionnaire, assignment to the owner, an implementation plan, tracking to closure with an evidence-based closure test, and a defined treatment where the obligation cannot be implemented in time, which is a documented risk acceptance rather than silence.

Reporting is where the board sees the value, and it should be exception-based. One page: how many obligations, how many tested this quarter, the exceptions by severity, anything past its remediation date, any change in the risk profile, and the decisions required. Not a narrative of the quarter's supervisory correspondence. The test of a good register at board level is that a committee member can see in ninety seconds whether the bank is exposed, and what they need to decide.

And be explicit that this is version one. Publish the known errors, the coverage gaps, the untested population and the maintenance cost, and put a plan for correction with a date. A register presented as complete invites trust that the evidence does not yet support; a register presented as a controlled baseline invites the engagement that will make it complete.
